title: Chapter 32
paragraphs: When Vronsky came back to the hotel, Anna wasn't home yet. Soon after he had left, he was told, some lady had come to see her, and she had gone out with the visitor. That she had gone out without saying where, that she still hadn't come back, and that all morning she had been off somewhere without a word to him — all this, together with the strange, keyed-up look on her face that morning, and his memory of the hostile tone in which she had almost snatched her son's photographs out of his hands in front of Yashvin, made him grave. He decided he absolutely had to have a frank talk with her. And he waited for her in her drawing room. But Anna didn't come back alone — she brought with her her old unmarried aunt, Princess Oblonskaya. This was the lady who had come in the morning and with whom Anna had gone out shopping. Anna appeared not to notice Vronsky's worried, questioning expression, and launched into a lively account of her morning's shopping. He could see that something was working in her; in her flashing eyes, when they rested on him for a moment, there was an intense focus, and in her words and gestures there was that nervous quickness and grace which, in the early days of their affair, had so enchanted him, but which now upset and alarmed him.

The table was set for four. Everyone was assembled and on the point of going into the small dining room when Tushkevitch turned up with a message from Princess Betsy. Princess Betsy begged Anna to excuse her for not having come to say good-bye in person; she had been unwell, but she asked Anna to come and see her between half past six and nine. Vronsky glanced at Anna over the precise time window — clearly designed so that she wouldn't meet anyone else — but Anna seemed not to notice it.
"So sorry, I can't make it between half past six and nine," she said with a faint smile.
"The princess will be very disappointed."
"And so am I."
"Are you going, perhaps, to hear Patti?" Tushkevitch asked.
"Patti? You put the idea in my head. I would go if it were possible to get a box."
"I can get one," Tushkevitch volunteered.
"I'd be very, very grateful to you," said Anna. "But won't you stay and dine with us?"

Vronsky gave a barely visible shrug. He was completely at a loss to understand what Anna was up to. Why had she brought the old Princess Oblonskaya home with her? Why had she pressed Tushkevitch to stay for dinner? And, most baffling of all, why was she sending him to fetch a box? Could she really be thinking, in her position, of going to Patti's gala, where every one of her acquaintances would be? He looked at her seriously, but she met his look with that defiant, half-mocking, half-desperate expression whose meaning he couldn't make out. At dinner Anna was in aggressively high spirits — she almost flirted with both Tushkevitch and Yashvin. When they got up from the table and Tushkevitch had gone off to secure a box at the opera, Yashvin went to smoke, and Vronsky went down with him to his own rooms. After sitting there for some time he ran back upstairs. Anna was already dressed in a low-cut gown of light silk and velvet she'd had made in Paris, with costly white lace on her head framing her face — particularly becoming, and showing off her dazzling beauty.
"Are you really going to the theater?" he said, trying not to look at her.
"Why do you ask in such an alarmed tone?" she said, hurt again by his not looking at her. "Why shouldn't I go?"
She gave every sign of not understanding why he was asking.
"Oh, no reason at all, of course," he said, frowning.
"That's just what I'm saying," she said, deliberately refusing to see the irony in his tone, and quietly turning back the cuff of her long, scented glove.
"Anna, for God's sake! What's the matter with you?" he said, appealing to her exactly the way her husband had once done.
"I don't understand what you're asking."
"You know it's out of the question to go."
"Why is it? I'm not going alone. Princess Varvara has gone to dress; she's going with me."
He shrugged with a look of bewilderment and despair.
"But do you mean to say you don't know?…" he began.

"But I don't want to know!" she almost shrieked. "I don't want to. Do I regret what I've done? No, no, no! If it were all to do over from the beginning, it would be exactly the same. For us — for you and me — there's only one thing that matters: whether we love each other. Other people aren't our concern. Why are we living here separately and not seeing each other? Why can't I go? I love you, and I don't care about anything else," she said in Russian, looking at him with a peculiar gleam in her eyes that he couldn't read. "If you haven't changed toward me, why aren't you looking at me?"
He looked at her. He saw all the beauty of her face and her full dress, which always suited her so well. But now her beauty and elegance were exactly what set him on edge.
"My feelings cannot change, you know that, but I beg you, I implore you," he said again in French, with a note of tender pleading in his voice but coldness in his eyes.
She didn't take in his words, but she saw the coldness in his eyes, and replied with irritation:
"And I'm asking you to explain why I shouldn't go."
"Because it might cause you…" he hesitated.
"I don't understand. Yashvin _n'est pas compromettant_, and Princess Varvara is no worse than anyone else. Oh, here she is!"

title: Chapter 33
paragraphs: For the first time Vronsky felt anger toward Anna, almost hatred for her for willfully refusing to understand her own position. The feeling was sharpened by the fact that he couldn't tell her plainly what was making him angry. If he had spoken his mind, he would have said:

"To show yourself at the theater in that dress, with a princess everyone already knows too much about, is not just an admission that you're a fallen woman — it's throwing down a challenge to society, which means cutting yourself off from it for good."

He couldn't say that to her. "But how can she fail to see it? What is going on inside her?" he asked himself. He felt at the same time that his respect for her had dropped while his sense of her beauty was sharper than ever.

He went back to his rooms scowling, and sitting down beside Yashvin — who had his long legs stretched out on a chair and was drinking brandy and seltzer water — he ordered a glass of the same for himself.

"You were talking about Lankovsky's Powerful. He's a fine horse, and I'd advise you to buy him," Yashvin said, glancing at his friend's gloomy face. "His hindquarters aren't quite first-rate, but the legs and head — you couldn't ask for better."
"I think I'll take him," Vronsky answered.
Their conversation about horses held his interest, but he didn't forget Anna for a moment, and he couldn't help listening for footsteps in the corridor and glancing at the clock on the mantelpiece.
"Anna Arkadyevna gave word to tell you she has gone to the theater."
Yashvin tipped another glass of brandy into the bubbling water, drank it down, and got up, buttoning his coat.
"Well, let's go," he said with a faint smile under his mustache, showing by that smile that he understood the source of Vronsky's gloom and wasn't attaching any importance to it.
"I'm not going," Vronsky said gloomily.
"Well, I have to. I promised. Good-bye, then. If you change your mind, come down to the stalls; you can take Kruzin's seat," Yashvin added as he went out.
"No, I have things to do."
"A wife is a burden, but it's worse when she's not actually a wife," Yashvin thought as he left the hotel.
Left alone, Vronsky got up from his chair and started pacing the room.

"What's today? The fourth night.… Yegor and his wife are there, and my mother, most likely. The whole of Petersburg, of course. Now she's gone in, taken off her cloak, stepped into the light. Tushkevitch, Yashvin, Princess Varvara," he pictured to himself. "And what about me? Either I look frightened or I've handed over to Tushkevitch the right to protect her. From every angle — stupid, stupid!… And why is she putting me in this position?" he said with a despairing gesture.

With that gesture he knocked into the table on which the seltzer water and the decanter of brandy were standing, and nearly upset it. He tried to catch it, let it slip, and angrily kicked the table over and rang the bell.
"If you want to stay in my service," he said to the valet who came in, "you'd better remember what your duties are. This shouldn't be sitting here. You should have cleared it."

The valet, conscious that he was in no way at fault, would have defended himself, but glancing at his master, he saw from his face that the only thing to do was keep silent. He hurriedly weaved his way among the pieces, dropped down on the carpet, and started picking up the unbroken and broken glasses and bottles.
"That's not your job. Send the waiter to clear up, and get my dress coat out."

Vronsky walked into the theater at half past eight. The performance was in full swing. The little old box-keeper recognized Vronsky as he helped him off with his fur coat, called him "Your Excellency," and suggested he not take a number but simply call for Fyodor. In the brightly lit corridor there was no one but the box-opener and two attendants with fur cloaks over their arms, listening at the doors. Through the closed doors came the discreet _staccato_ of the orchestra and a single female voice carrying a musical phrase distinctly. The door opened to let the box-opener slip through, and the phrase, coming to a close, reached Vronsky's ear clearly. But the doors closed again at once, and Vronsky didn't hear the end of the phrase or the cadence of the accompaniment, though he could tell from the thunder of applause that it was over. When he came into the hall, brilliantly lit with chandeliers and gas jets, the noise was still going on. On stage the singer, bowing and smiling, with bare shoulders glittering with diamonds, was — with the help of the tenor, who had given her his arm — gathering up the bouquets that kept landing awkwardly over the footlights. Then she went up to a gentleman with glossy pomaded hair parted down the middle, who was leaning across the footlights holding something out to her, and the entire audience in the stalls as well as in the boxes was on edge, craning forward, shouting and clapping. The conductor in his high chair helped pass the offering along and straightened his white tie. Vronsky walked into the middle of the stalls and stood there, looking around. That evening, less than ever, was his attention on the familiar, usual surroundings — the stage, the noise, the whole familiar, uninteresting, multicolored herd of spectators packing the theater.

There were, as always, the same sort of ladies with the same sort of officers at the back of the boxes; the same gaily dressed women — God knows who — and uniforms and black coats; the same dirty crowd in the upper gallery; and among them, in the boxes and the front rows, some forty of the _real_ people. It was to those oases that Vronsky directed his attention right away, and with them he entered straight into communication.

The act was over when he came in, so instead of going straight to his brother's box he went to the front row of the stalls and stopped at the footlights with Serpuhovskoy, who, standing with one knee raised and his heel resting on the footlights, had spotted him in the distance and beckoned him over with a smile.

Vronsky still hadn't seen Anna. He was deliberately not looking in her direction. But from the way people's eyes were turned, he knew where she was. He looked round discreetly, but he wasn't looking for her; expecting the worst, his eyes were searching for Alexey Alexandrovitch. To his relief, Alexey Alexandrovitch was not in the theater that evening.
"How little of the soldier is left in you!" Serpuhovskoy was telling him. "A diplomat, an artist, something of that kind, you'd say."
"Yes, putting on a black coat was like coming home," Vronsky answered, smiling and slowly taking out his opera glass.
"Well, I'll admit I envy you that. When I get back from abroad and put this on," he touched his epaulets, "I miss my freedom."
Serpuhovskoy had long since given up hope of Vronsky's career, but he liked him as much as ever, and was being particularly warm to him now.
"What a shame you weren't in time for the first act!"

Vronsky, listening with one ear, swung his opera glass off the stalls and over the boxes. Near a lady in a turban and a bald old man — who seemed to wave angrily in the moving lens — Vronsky suddenly caught sight of Anna's head, proud, strikingly beautiful, and smiling, framed in lace. She was in the fifth box, twenty paces from him. She was sitting toward the front, and, turning slightly, was saying something to Yashvin. The set of her head on her handsome, broad shoulders, and the restrained excitement and brilliance of her eyes and her whole face, reminded him of her exactly as he had seen her at the ball in Moscow. But what he felt now toward her beauty was completely different. In his feeling for her now there was nothing of mystery, and so her beauty, though it drew him even more intensely than before, now gave him a sense of injury. She wasn't looking in his direction, but Vronsky could tell that she had already seen him.

When Vronsky turned the glass back that way, he noticed that Princess Varvara was unusually red and kept laughing in an unnatural way, glancing over at the neighboring box. Anna, folding her fan and tapping it against the red velvet, was looking somewhere else and didn't see — and clearly didn't want to see — what was going on in the next box. Yashvin's face wore the look it usually had when he was losing at cards. Scowling, he sucked the left end of his mustache further and further into his mouth, and kept casting sidelong glances at the next box.

In that box on the left were the Kartasovs. Vronsky knew them, and knew that Anna knew them too. Madame Kartasova, a thin little woman, was standing up in her box with her back turned toward Anna, putting on a mantle her husband was holding for her. Her face was pale and angry, and she was talking heatedly. Kartasov, a fat, bald man, kept looking back at Anna while trying to calm his wife. Once his wife had walked out, the husband lingered for a long time, trying to catch Anna's eye, plainly wanting to bow to her. But Anna, with unmistakable deliberateness, refused to notice him, and went on talking to Yashvin, whose cropped head was leaning down toward her. Kartasov left without making his bow, and the box was empty.

Vronsky couldn't make out exactly what had passed between the Kartasovs and Anna, but he could see that something humiliating for Anna had happened. He knew this both from what he had seen, and most of all from Anna's face — she was, he could tell, straining every nerve to play through the part she had set herself. And in keeping up that outward composure she was completely successful. Anyone who didn't know her and her circle, who hadn't heard all the things the women had been saying about her in tones of pity, indignation, and astonishment — that she should show herself in society, and so conspicuously, with her lace and her beauty — would have admired the calm and loveliness of this woman without the faintest suspicion that she was feeling like a man in the stocks.

Knowing that something had happened but not knowing exactly what, Vronsky felt a stab of agonizing anxiety, and hoping to find out something, he started toward his brother's box. Deliberately taking the route furthest from Anna's box, he ran on his way out into the colonel of his old regiment, who was talking to two acquaintances. Vronsky heard the name Madame Karenina, and noticed how quickly the colonel addressed Vronsky loudly by name, with a meaningful glance at his companions.
"Ah, Vronsky! When are you coming back to the regiment? We can't let you off without a supper. You're one of the old set," said the colonel of his regiment.
"I can't stop now, awfully sorry — another time," Vronsky said, and ran upstairs toward his brother's box.
The old countess, Vronsky's mother, with her steel-gray curls, was in his brother's box. Varya, with the young Princess Sorokina, met him in the corridor.
Leaving Princess Sorokina with her mother, Varya held out her hand to her brother-in-law and immediately started talking about what was on his mind. He had never seen her so agitated.
"I think it's mean and hateful, and Madame Kartasova had no right to do it. Madame Karenina…" she began.
"But what is it? I don't know."
"What? You haven't heard?"
"You know I'd be the last person to hear about it."
"There isn't a more spiteful creature than that Madame Kartasova!"
"But what did she do?"

"My husband told me.… She insulted Madame Karenina. Her husband started talking to her across the box, and Madame Kartasova made a scene. She said something out loud, he says — something insulting — and walked out."
"Count, your maman is asking for you," said the young Princess Sorokina, peering out from the door of the box.
"I've been waiting for you the whole time," said his mother, smiling sarcastically. "You were nowhere to be seen."
Her son saw that she couldn't suppress a smile of pleasure.
"Good evening, maman. I was just coming to you," he said coldly.
"Why aren't you going to _faire la cour à Madame Karenina?_" she went on, when Princess Sorokina had moved away. "_Elle fait sensation. On oublie la Patti pour elle_."
"Maman, I've asked you not to talk to me about that," he answered, scowling.
"I'm only saying what everyone is saying."
Vronsky didn't answer, and after a few words to Princess Sorokina he left. At the door he ran into his brother.
"Ah, Alexey!" his brother said. "How disgusting! An idiot of a woman, nothing else.… I was about to go straight to her. Come, let's go together."

Vronsky wasn't listening. With quick steps he went downstairs; he felt he had to do something, but he didn't know what. Anger with her for having put herself and him in such a false position, combined with pity for her suffering, filled his heart. He went down and walked straight to Anna's box. At her box stood Stremov, talking to her.
"There are no tenors anymore. _Le moule en est brisé!_"
Vronsky bowed to her and stopped to greet Stremov.
"You came in late, I think, and missed the best song," Anna said to Vronsky, glancing at him, he thought, ironically.
"I'm a poor judge of music," he said, looking sternly at her.
"Like Prince Yashvin," she said with a smile, "who thinks Patti sings too loud."

"Thank you," she said, her small hand in its long glove taking the playbill Vronsky had picked up — and suddenly, at that instant, her lovely face quivered. She got up and went into the back of the box.
When in the next act he noticed her box was empty, Vronsky, drawing indignant "hushes" from the silent audience, walked out in the middle of a solo and drove home.

Anna was already at home. When Vronsky went up to her, she was still in the dress she had worn at the theater. She was sitting in the first armchair against the wall, staring straight in front of her. She looked at him, and at once resumed her former position.
"Anna," he said.
"You — you are to blame for everything!" she cried, with tears of despair and hatred in her voice, getting up.
"I begged you, I implored you not to go. I knew it would be unpleasant.…"
"Unpleasant!" she cried. "Hideous! As long as I live I'll never forget it. She said it was a disgrace to sit beside me."
"Silly woman's chatter," he said. "But why risk it, why provoke it?…"
"I hate your calm. You ought never to have brought me to this. If you loved me.…"
"Anna! How does my love come into it?"
"Oh, if you loved me the way I love, if you were tortured the way I am!…" she said, looking at him with a frightened expression.
He felt sorry for her, and angry all the same. He assured her of his love because he saw it was the only way to calm her, and he didn't reproach her out loud, but in his heart he reproached her.
And the protestations of love that struck him as so trite he was embarrassed to say them, she drank in eagerly, and gradually grew calmer. The next day, fully reconciled, they left for the country.
PART SIX

title: Chapter 1
paragraphs: Darya Alexandrovna spent the summer with her children at Pokrovskoe, at her sister Kitty Levin's. Her own estate was practically a ruin, and the Levins had pressed her to spend the season with them. Stepan Arkadyevitch heartily approved. He kept saying how sorry he was that his official duties kept him from spending the whole summer in the country with his family — which would have been his greatest happiness — and so he stayed in Moscow and came down for a day or two now and then. Beyond the Oblonskys, with all their children and their governess, the old princess had also come for the summer; she felt it her duty to keep an eye on her inexperienced daughter in her _interesting condition_. On top of that, Varenka, Kitty's friend from abroad, had kept her promise to visit Kitty once she was married and had come to stay. Every one of these guests was a friend or relative of Levin's wife. He liked them all, but he still missed his own Levin world and Levin ways, which were being smothered under this incoming tide of what he privately called the "Shtcherbatsky element." Of his own relations, only Sergey Ivanovitch was staying with him, and even he was cast in the Koznishev rather than the Levin mold, so that the Levin spirit had been thoroughly drowned out.

The Levins' house, empty for so long, was now so full that nearly every room was occupied, and almost every day, sitting down at table, the old princess counted heads and had to set the thirteenth grandchild at a separate table. And Kitty, careful housekeeper that she was, had no small trouble keeping the place supplied with chickens, turkeys, and geese — so many were needed to satisfy the summer appetites of guests and children.

The whole family was at dinner. Dolly's children, along with their governess and Varenka, were planning a mushroom-hunting expedition. Sergey Ivanovitch, whom the rest of the company regarded with a near-reverence for his intellect and learning, startled everyone by joining the mushroom conversation.
"Take me along. I'm very fond of mushroom-picking," he said, looking at Varenka. "It strikes me as a delightful pastime."

"We'd be glad to have you," Varenka answered, coloring slightly. Kitty and Dolly traded a meaningful glance. The fact that the learned, intellectual Sergey Ivanovitch wanted to go mushroom-picking with Varenka confirmed certain theories of Kitty's that her mind had been chewing on lately. She hurried to say something to her mother so that nobody would catch the look. After dinner Sergey Ivanovitch took his coffee to the drawing-room window, and while he carried on a conversation with his brother he kept an eye on the door through which the children would head out for their expedition. Levin sat at the next window beside him.
Kitty stood next to her husband, clearly waiting for the end of a conversation that did not interest her so that she could tell him something.

"You've changed in many ways since you married, and all for the better," Sergey Ivanovitch said with a smile to Kitty, plainly not very absorbed in the talk, "but you've kept that loyalty of yours to the most paradoxical theories."
"Katya, it isn't good for you to stand," her husband told her, setting a chair for her and giving her a meaningful look.
"And there's no time anyway," Sergey Ivanovitch added, seeing the children come running.
At the head of them all came Tanya, her stockings drawn tight, galloping sideways with a basket in one hand and Sergey Ivanovitch's hat in the other. She ran straight up to him.
Walking boldly up to Sergey Ivanovitch with shining eyes — so like her father's fine eyes — she handed him his hat and made as if to put it on for him, softening her cheek with a shy, friendly smile.
"Varenka's waiting," she said, carefully fitting the hat on, gathering from Sergey Ivanovitch's smile that she had permission to.
Varenka was standing in the doorway in a yellow print dress with a white kerchief on her head.
"Coming, coming, Varvara Andreevna," said Sergey Ivanovitch, finishing his cup of coffee and tucking his handkerchief and cigar-case into separate pockets.

"Isn't my Varenka sweet? Well?" Kitty said to her husband the moment Sergey Ivanovitch stood up. She pitched her voice so that Sergey Ivanovitch would hear, and meant him to. "And how good-looking — such a refined beauty! Varenka!" Kitty called out. "Will you be in the mill copse? We'll come out and meet you there."
"You really do forget your condition, Kitty," said the old princess, hurrying out through the door. "You mustn't shout like that."

Hearing Kitty's voice and her mother's scolding, Varenka came over to Kitty with quick, light steps. The rapidity of her movement, her flushed and eager face — everything betrayed that something out of the ordinary was happening in her. Kitty knew what it was; she had been watching her closely. She had called Varenka over now only to give her, silently, a blessing for the great event which, as Kitty imagined it, was bound to happen that day after dinner in the wood.
"Varenka, I'd be very happy if a certain something were to happen," she whispered as she kissed her.
"And are you coming with us?" Varenka said to Levin in confusion, pretending she had not heard what had been said.
"I'm coming, but only as far as the threshing-floor — I'll stop there."
"What do you want there?" Kitty asked.
"I have to take a look at the new wagons, and check the invoice," Levin said. "And where will you be?"
"On the terrace."

title: Chapter 2
paragraphs: All the ladies of the party were gathered on the terrace. They liked sitting there after dinner anyway, and that day they had work to do there too. Beyond the usual sewing and knitting of baby clothes — which they were all busy with — jam was being made on the terrace that afternoon by a method new to Agafea Mihalovna: without any added water. Kitty had brought the method with her from her own family. Agafea Mihalovna, who had always been entrusted with the jam-making and who took it for granted that whatever was done in the Levin household must be right, had nevertheless slipped water in with the strawberries, insisting jam couldn't be made without it. She had been caught at it, and now she was making the jam in front of everybody, and was to be shown conclusively that it could be done perfectly well without water.

Agafea Mihalovna, her face heated and angry, her hair coming undone, her thin arms bare to the elbow, was tilting the preserving-pan over the charcoal stove, glowering at the raspberries and quietly praying they'd stick and refuse to cook. The princess, well aware that Agafea Mihalovna's wrath was aimed mainly at her — the person ultimately responsible for the raspberry experiment — tried to look engrossed in other things and indifferent to the jam, kept up an unrelated conversation, and stole sideways glances toward the stove.

"I always buy my maids' dresses myself, out of some cheap material," the princess said, picking up the thread of an earlier conversation. "Isn't it time to skim it, my dear?" she added to Agafea Mihalovna. "There's no need at all for you to do it, and it's too hot for you," she said, heading Kitty off.

"I'll do it," said Dolly, and getting up she ran the spoon carefully through the foaming sugar, knocking the spoon now and then against a plate to shake off the clinging jam — a plate already coated with yellow-red scum and blood-colored syrup. "How they'll enjoy this at tea!" she thought of her children, remembering how she had wondered as a child why on earth grown-ups didn't eat the best part — the scum.
"Stiva says it's much better to give them money." Dolly meanwhile took up the weighty question of what to give the servants as presents. "But...."
"Money is out of the question!" the princess and Kitty said in one breath. "They appreciate a real present...."
"Last year, for instance, I bought our Matrona Semyenovna — not poplin, but something along those lines," said the princess.
"I remember, she was wearing it on your name-day."
"A charming pattern — so simple and refined. I'd have liked it for myself, if she hadn't already had it. Something like Varenka's. So pretty, and not expensive."
"Well, I think it's done now," said Dolly, letting syrup drip from the spoon.
"When it sets as it drops, it's ready. Cook it a little longer, Agafea Mihalovna."
"The flies!" said Agafea Mihalovna crossly. "It'll come out the same in the end," she added.
"Oh, isn't it sweet! Don't scare it!" Kitty said suddenly, watching a sparrow that had landed on the step and was pecking at the heart of a raspberry.
"Yes, but keep back a bit from the stove," said her mother.

"_À propos de Varenka_," said Kitty, switching into French, as they had been doing throughout so that Agafea Mihalovna wouldn't follow them, "do you know, mamma, somehow I feel things will be settled today. You know what I mean. Wouldn't it be wonderful!"
"What a brilliant matchmaker she is, though!" said Dolly. "How carefully, how skillfully she nudges them together!..."
"No, tell me, mamma, what do you think?"

"What is one supposed to think? He" (by _he_ she meant Sergey Ivanovitch) "could have been a match at any time for anyone in Russia. Now, of course, he's no longer a young man, but I know plenty of girls who would gladly marry him even today.... She's a very nice girl, but he could...."
"No, mamma, do try to see why, for him and for her too, nothing better could be imagined. To begin with, she's charming!" said Kitty, ticking off a finger.
"He certainly finds her very attractive — that much is plain," Dolly agreed.
"Then his position in society is such that he doesn't need to look for either money or rank in a wife. All he needs is a good, sweet wife — a peaceful one."
"With her he certainly would have peace," Dolly agreed.

"Thirdly, that she should love him. And that's exactly how it is... I mean, that's exactly how it could be! I can't wait to see them coming out of the wood — with everything settled. I'll know the moment I look in their eyes. I'd be so happy! What do you think, Dolly?"
"Now don't work yourself up. It's not at all good for you to get worked up," her mother said.
"I'm not worked up, mamma. I have a feeling he'll propose to her today."

"It really is strange, how and when a man makes an offer.... There's a sort of barrier, and then all at once it's down," said Dolly, with a thoughtful smile, remembering her own past with Stepan Arkadyevitch.
"Mamma, how did papa propose to you?" Kitty asked suddenly.
"Nothing out of the ordinary — it was very simple," the princess answered, but her face shone all over at the memory.
"But how? You were in love with him already, before you were even allowed to speak together?"
Kitty was getting a particular pleasure out of being able to talk to her mother as an equal now, about questions that mattered so deeply in a woman's life.
"Of course I was; he had come to stay with us in the country."
"But how did it actually get settled between you, mamma?"
"You probably think you invented something completely new? It's always the same: it gets settled by glances, by smiles...."
"How nicely you put that, mamma! It really is glances and smiles that do it," Dolly agreed.
"But what did he actually say?"
"What did Kostya say to you?"
"He wrote it down in chalk. It was wonderful.... How long ago it all feels!" she said.

And all three women fell to thinking about the same thing. Kitty was the first to break the silence. She was remembering everything from the last winter before her marriage — her infatuation with Vronsky.

"There's just one thing... that old affair of Varenka's," she said, brought to it by a natural train of thought. "I would have liked to say something to Sergey Ivanovitch, to prepare him. They're all — all men, I mean," she added, "awfully jealous about our past."
"Not all of them," Dolly said. "You're judging by your own husband. Even now it makes him wretched just to remember Vronsky. Isn't that true?"
"Yes," Kitty answered, a thoughtful smile in her eyes.

"Really, though, I don't see," their mother put in, defending her own motherly care of her daughter, "what there was in your past that could trouble him? That Vronsky paid you attention — that happens to every girl."
"Oh, but that's not what we meant," Kitty said, flushing a little.
"No, let me finish," her mother went on. "You yourself wouldn't let me have a word with Vronsky. Don't you remember?"
"Oh, mamma!" Kitty said, with a pained look.

"There's no holding you young people back nowadays.... Your friendship couldn't have gone past the bounds of propriety. I would have spoken to him myself, called him to account. But, darling, you mustn't get agitated. Please remember that and calm down."
"I'm perfectly calm, maman."

"How lucky it was for Kitty that Anna came along then," said Dolly, "and how unlucky for Anna. It's come out exactly the other way round," she added, struck by her own thought. "Then Anna was so happy and Kitty thought herself miserable. Now it's the reverse. I think of her often."
"What a person to spend your thoughts on! A vile, hateful woman with no heart," said her mother, who could not forgive the fact that Kitty had married Levin and not Vronsky.

"Why do you want to talk about it?" Kitty said, annoyed. "I don't think about it, and I don't want to think about it.... I don't want to think about it," she repeated, catching the familiar sound of her husband's step on the terrace stairs.
"What is it you don't want to think about?" Levin asked, coming onto the terrace.
Nobody answered him, and he didn't ask again.
"Sorry to have broken in on your ladies' parliament," he said, glancing around discontentedly and sensing that they'd been talking about something they wouldn't talk about in front of him.

For a moment he felt he was sharing Agafea Mihalovna's mood — her irritation at the jam being made without water, and at the whole outside Shtcherbatsky influence in general. But he smiled and went over to Kitty.
"Well, how are you?" he asked, looking at her with the expression everyone wore when they looked at her these days.
"Oh, very well," Kitty said with a smile. "And how did things go for you?"
"The wagons hold three times what the old carts did. Well, shall we go and collect the children? I've ordered the horses harnessed."
"What? You want to take Kitty in the wagonette?" her mother said reproachfully.
"At a walking pace, princess."

Levin never called the princess "maman," the way men often address their mothers-in-law, and the princess minded that he didn't. But fond and respectful of her as Levin was, he couldn't bring himself to use the word without feeling he was profaning his feeling for his own dead mother.
"Come with us, maman," said Kitty.
"I don't like watching such recklessness."
"All right, I'll walk then, I feel so well." Kitty stood up, went over to her husband, and took his hand.
"You may feel well, but everything in moderation," the princess said.
"Well, Agafea Mihalovna, is the jam ready?" said Levin, smiling at her, trying to lift her mood. "Has it worked out the new way?"
"I suppose it's all right. By our reckoning it's been boiled too long."

"It'll be all the better for that, Agafea Mihalovna — it won't go moldy, even now that our ice is already thawing, so we've no cool cellar to store it in," Kitty said, instantly catching her husband's purpose and addressing the old housekeeper in the same spirit. "But your pickles are so good — mamma says she's never tasted any like them," she added, smiling and straightening her kerchief.
Agafea Mihalovna looked angrily at Kitty.
"You needn't go consoling me, mistress. I only have to look at you with him and I feel happy," she said, and something in the rough familiarity of that _with him_ touched Kitty.
"Come with us, look for mushrooms — you'll show us the best spots." Agafea Mihalovna smiled and shook her head, as if to say: "I'd like to be angry with you, too, but I can't."
"Do it the way I told you, please," said the princess. "Put paper over the jam, soak it with a little rum, and even without ice it will never mildew."

title: Chapter 3
paragraphs: Kitty was particularly glad of the chance to be alone with her husband, because she had noticed the flicker of hurt that had crossed his face — always so quick to register every feeling — at the moment when he had come onto the terrace and asked what they were talking about and gotten no answer.

When they had walked off ahead of the others and were out of sight of the house, on the beaten dusty road marked by rusty wheel-ruts and sprinkled with grains of corn, she pressed closer against his arm and held it tighter to her. He had already forgotten the brief sting of that moment, and alone with her, with the thought of her approaching motherhood never out of his mind for an instant, he felt a new and delicious happiness — pure, with no admixture of sensual feeling — in being close to the woman he loved. There was no need for talk, and yet he wanted to hear her voice, which, like her eyes, had changed since she had been carrying the child. In her voice, as in her eyes, there was a softness and seriousness that belongs to people steadily absorbed in one cherished pursuit.
"You're not tired? Lean on me more," he said.
"No, I'm so glad to be alone with you — and I have to admit, even though I'm happy with everyone here, I do miss our winter evenings just to ourselves."
"Those were good. This is even better. Both are better," he said, squeezing her hand.
"Do you know what we were talking about when you came in?"
"About jam?"
"About jam, yes, but afterwards about how men propose."

"Ah!" Levin said, listening more to the sound of her voice than to the words, and keeping an eye on the path, which was now running through the forest, steering her past spots where she might stumble.
"And about Sergey Ivanovitch and Varenka. You've noticed?... I'm very keen for it," she went on. "What do you think?" And she glanced up at his face.
"I don't know what to think," Levin answered with a smile. "Sergey strikes me as very strange in that way. I told you, you remember...."
"Yes, that he was in love with that girl who died...."

"That was when I was a child; I know it only from hearsay, from stories told later. I remember him then. He was wonderfully kind. But I've watched him with women since; he is friendly, he likes some of them, but you can feel that to him they're just people, not women."
"Yes, but now, with Varenka... I get the sense there's something there...."
"Maybe there is.... But you have to know him.... He's a strange, remarkable person. He lives a purely spiritual life. He's too pure and too lofty a nature."
"What — would this bring him down, then?"
"No, but he's so used to a spiritual life that he can't reconcile himself to actual fact, and Varenka is, after all, actual fact."

By now Levin had gotten used to stating his thoughts out loud without bothering to clothe them in precise language. He knew that his wife, in moments of tender intimacy like this one, would catch his meaning from a hint, and she did.
"Yes, but there's not as much actual fact about her as there is about me. I can see that he would never have cared for me. She's entirely spiritual."
"Oh no, he's very fond of you — and I'm always so glad when my family takes to you...."
"Yes, he's very nice to me, but...."

"It's not like it was with poor Nikolay... the two of you really cared for each other," Levin finished. "Why not talk about him?" he added. "Sometimes I blame myself for not — it ends with you simply forgetting. Ah, how dreadful and how dear he was!... Well, what were we talking about?" Levin said after a pause.
"You think he can't fall in love," Kitty said, translating into her own terms.
"It isn't so much that he can't fall in love," Levin said, smiling, "but he doesn't have the weakness you need for it.... I've always envied him, and even now, happy as I am, I still envy him."
"You envy him for not being able to fall in love?"
"I envy him for being a better man than I am," Levin said. "He doesn't live for himself. His whole life is subordinated to duty. That's why he can be calm and content."
"And you?" Kitty asked, with a teasing, loving smile.

She could never have explained the chain of thought that lay behind that smile; but the final link in it was that her husband, by raising his brother and putting himself down, wasn't being entirely honest. Kitty knew that the dishonesty came from his love for his brother, from a sense of shame at being too happy, and above all from his constant hunger to be better — and she loved that in him, so she smiled.
"And you? What are you so dissatisfied with?" she asked, with the same smile.
Her disbelief in his self-dissatisfaction delighted him, and without meaning to, he tried to draw out of her the grounds for that disbelief.
"I'm happy, but I'm dissatisfied with myself..." he said.
"But how can you be dissatisfied if you're happy?"

"Well, how shall I put it?... Deep down I care about nothing in the world except that you don't stumble — do you see? Oh, but really, you mustn't skip about like that!" he broke off to scold her for too quick a step over a branch lying in the path. "But when I think about myself, and compare myself with others — especially my brother — I feel I'm a poor creature."
"How so?" Kitty pursued with the same smile. "Don't you work for others too? What about your cooperative settlement, your work on the estate, your book?..."

"No, I feel — and especially right now, and it's your fault," he said, pressing her hand, "that none of that counts. I'm doing it all half-heartedly. If only I could care about all of that the way I care about you!... Instead I do it these days like a task I've been set."
"Well, what would you say about papa, then?" Kitty asked. "Is he a poor creature too, because he doesn't do anything for the public good?"

"Your father? No! For that you need the simplicity, the straightforwardness, the goodness your father has — and I don't have that. I do nothing and then fret about it. It's all your fault. Before there was you — and _this_ as well," he added, with a glance at her waist she understood, "I poured all my energy into work. Now I can't, and I'm ashamed; I do it as though it were homework I've been assigned, just going through the motions...."

"Well — but would you change places with Sergey Ivanovitch this minute?" Kitty asked. "Would you like to do that kind of public-good work, and love your assignment the way he does, and have nothing else?"
"Of course not," Levin said. "But I'm so happy I don't understand anything. So you really think he'll propose to her today?" he added after a short silence.

"I do, and I don't. But I'm desperately keen for it. Here, wait a moment." She stooped and picked a wild camomile by the edge of the path. "Now count: he proposes, he doesn't," she said, handing him the flower.
"He does, he doesn't," Levin said, plucking off the white petals.
"No, no!" Kitty said, catching at his hand to stop him. She had been watching his fingers attentively. "You took off two at once."
"All right — look, this little one won't count, to make up for it," said Levin, picking off a small half-grown petal. "Here's the wagonette catching up with us."
"Aren't you tired, Kitty?" the princess called.
"Not the least bit."
"If you are, hop in — the horses are quiet and barely walking."
But there was no point getting in; they were almost there, and they all walked on together.

title: Chapter 4
paragraphs: Varenka, the white kerchief over her black hair, surrounded by the children, looking after them gaily and good-naturedly while clearly keyed up at the possibility of receiving a proposal from the man she cared about, was very attractive. Sergey Ivanovitch walked beside her without taking his eyes off her. Looking at her, he ran through every charming thing he had heard her say, every good thing he knew about her, and grew more and more conscious that what he felt for her was something special, something he had only felt once before, long ago, in his early youth. The happiness of being near her kept building, and at last reached the point where, as he laid an enormous, slender-stemmed agaric in her basket, he looked straight into her face and, seeing the flush of glad, alarmed excitement that spread over her, was thrown himself, and smiled at her in silence a smile that said too much.
"If that's how it is," he said to himself, "I ought to think it through and make up my mind, not give in like a schoolboy to the impulse of a moment."

"I'll go off and pick by myself, otherwise my efforts won't show," he said, and stepped away from the edge of the forest, where they had been walking on low silky grass between widely spaced old birches, and pushed deeper into the wood, where between the white birch trunks stood gray aspen trunks and dark hazel bushes. After about forty paces Sergey Ivanovitch, knowing he was out of sight, came to a stop behind a bushy spindle-tree in full flower with its rosy-red catkins. It was perfectly quiet all around him. Only overhead, in the birches he was standing under, the flies kept up a steady buzzing like a swarm of bees, and from time to time the children's voices drifted across to him. All at once he heard, not far from the edge of the wood, the sound of Varenka's contralto voice calling out to Grisha, and a smile of pleasure crossed Sergey Ivanovitch's face. Catching himself smiling, he shook his head disapprovingly at his own state, took out a cigar, and started to light it. For a long while he couldn't get a match to strike against the trunk of a birch — the soft scales of the white bark rubbed the phosphorus off, and the flame kept going out. Finally one of the matches caught, and the fragrant cigar smoke, hanging in unsteady, flat, wide coils, drifted forward and upward over a bush under the overhanging birch branches. Watching the streak of smoke, Sergey Ivanovitch walked slowly on, thinking over his situation.

"Why not?" he thought. "If it were only a passing infatuation or some passion, if it were only this attraction — this mutual attraction (I can call it a _mutual_ attraction), but if I felt it was at odds with the whole direction of my life — if I felt that by giving in to this attraction I'd be betraying my vocation and my duty... but it isn't so. The one thing I can hold against it is that, when I lost Marie, I told myself I'd stay faithful to her memory. That's the one thing I can hold against this feeling.... That's a serious thing," Sergey Ivanovitch said to himself, while feeling at the same time that this consideration had not the slightest weight for him personally, and could only, at most, take something away from his romantic image in other people's eyes. "But beyond that, however hard I look, I can find nothing to say against this feeling. If I were choosing by suitability alone, I couldn't have found anyone better."

However many women and girls he ran through in his mind, he couldn't think of a single one who combined to such a degree all — absolutely all — the qualities he wanted in a wife. She had all the charm and freshness of youth, but she was no longer a child; and if she loved him, she loved him consciously, the way a woman should love. That was one thing. Second: she was not only far from being a creature of society, she had a clear distaste for society life, and at the same time she knew the world and had all the manners of a woman of the best society — which Sergey Ivanovitch considered indispensable in the woman who was to share his life. Third: she was religious — and not as a child, unconsciously religious and good, the way Kitty for instance was, but with a life built on religious principles. Even in small matters, Sergey Ivanovitch found in her everything he wanted in a wife: she was poor and alone in the world, so she wouldn't bring along the mass of relatives and their influence he saw now in Kitty's case. She would owe everything to her husband — exactly what he had always wanted for his own future family life. And this girl, who united all these qualities, loved him. He was a modest man, but he couldn't help seeing it. And he loved her. There was one thing against it — his age. But he came from a long-lived family; he hadn't a single gray hair; no one would have taken him for forty; and he remembered Varenka's saying that it was only in Russia that men of fifty thought of themselves as old, and that in France a man of fifty considered himself _dans la force de l'âge_, and a man of forty was _un jeune homme_. What did the bare count of years matter when he felt as young at heart as he had twenty years ago? Wasn't it youth to feel the way he was feeling now, as he came out from the other side of the wood to the edge and saw, in the warm light of slanting sun, the graceful figure of Varenka in her yellow dress with her basket, walking lightly past the trunk of an old birch — and when the sight of her blended so perfectly with the beauty of the view, the yellow oat-field lying under the slanting light, and beyond it the distant ancient forest flecked with yellow and dissolving into blue distance? His heart pounded with joy. A softened feeling came over him. He had made up his mind. Varenka, who had just crouched down to pick a mushroom, rose with a supple movement and looked around. Throwing the cigar away, Sergey Ivanovitch walked toward her with resolute steps.

title: Chapter 5
paragraphs: "Varvara Andreevna, when I was very young I set up in my mind the ideal of the woman I would love and be happy to call my wife. I have lived a long life, and now, for the first time, I have met what I was looking for — in you. I love you, and I offer you my hand."
Sergey Ivanovitch was saying this to himself as he closed the last ten paces between him and Varvara. She was kneeling, hands held over the mushrooms to keep Grisha off them, calling little Masha.
"Come over here, little ones! There are so many!" she was saying in her sweet, deep voice.
Seeing Sergey Ivanovitch coming up, she didn't stand or change her position, but everything about her told him she felt his presence and was glad of it.
"Well, did you find any?" she asked from under the white kerchief, turning her handsome, softly smiling face to him.
"Not one," Sergey Ivanovitch said. "Did you?"
She didn't answer; the children were swarming around her.

"That one too, near the twig," she pointed out to little Masha — a small mushroom split across its rosy cap by a dry stalk of grass it had pushed up through. Varenka got up while Masha picked it, breaking it into two white halves. "This takes me back to my childhood," she added, moving away from the children to Sergey Ivanovitch's side.

They walked on for a few steps in silence. Varenka could see that he wanted to speak; she could guess about what, and felt faint with joy and panic. They had walked far enough that no one could hear them now, but still he didn't start. It would have been better if Varenka had stayed silent. After a stretch of silence it would have been easier to say what they wanted to say than after talking about mushrooms. But against her own will, as if by accident, Varenka said:

"So you didn't find anything? Though there are always fewer in the middle of the wood." Sergey Ivanovitch sighed and didn't answer. He was annoyed that she had brought up mushrooms again. He wanted to circle her back to those first words about her childhood; but after a long pause, as though against his own will, he made a remark in response to her last words.
"I've heard the white edible funguses are mostly found at the edge of the wood, though I can't tell them apart."

A few more minutes passed; they moved still further from the children and were quite alone. Varenka's heart was pounding so hard she could hear it, and she felt herself turning red, then pale, then red again.

To be the wife of a man like Koznishev, after her time with Madame Stahl, struck her imagination as the height of happiness. On top of that, she was almost sure she was in love with him. And it had to be decided in the next minute. She was frightened. She dreaded both his speaking and his not speaking.

Now or never the thing had to be said — Sergey Ivanovitch felt that too. Everything in Varenka's expression — the flushed cheeks, the lowered eyes — betrayed an agonizing suspense. Sergey Ivanovitch saw it and felt sorry for her. He even felt that to say nothing now would be an insult to her. Quickly, in his head, he ran through all the arguments for his decision. He even went over the words in which he meant to put his proposal — but instead of those words, some entirely unexpected thought that drifted into his head made him ask:
"What's the difference between a 'birch' mushroom and a 'white' mushroom?"
Varenka's lips trembled as she answered:
"In the cap there's hardly any difference — it's in the stalk."

And the instant the words were out, both of them felt that it was over, that what was supposed to be said would not be said; and the emotion that had been mounting in them up until then began to subside.
"The stalk of a birch mushroom looks like a dark man's chin after two days without shaving," Sergey Ivanovitch said, now speaking quite calmly.

"Yes, that's true," Varenka answered with a smile, and without realizing it they had changed direction. They were beginning to head back toward the children. Varenka felt sore and ashamed; at the same time she was relieved.
Once he was home again and went back over the whole thing, Sergey Ivanovitch decided his earlier resolution had been a mistake. He couldn't be unfaithful to Marie's memory.
"Gently, children, gently!" Levin shouted, almost angrily, at the children, planting himself in front of his wife to shield her as the pack came flying toward them with shrieks of delight.

Behind the children Sergey Ivanovitch and Varenka came out of the wood. Kitty didn't need to ask Varenka anything; from the calm, somewhat crestfallen faces of the two of them she could see that her plan had not come off.
"Well?" her husband asked her as they were heading home.
"It doesn't bite," Kitty said, her smile and her way of speaking recalling her father — a likeness Levin often noticed with pleasure.
"How doesn't it bite?"
"Like this," she said, taking her husband's hand, lifting it to her mouth, and just barely brushing it with closed lips. "Like a kiss on a priest's hand."
"Which side didn't it bite on?" he asked, laughing.
"Both sides. But it should have been like this...."
"There are peasants coming...."
"Oh, they didn't see."

title: Chapter 6
paragraphs: While the children were having their tea, the grown-ups sat on the balcony and talked as though nothing had happened — even though they all knew, and Sergey Ivanovitch and Varenka knew it especially well, that something had in fact happened which, though it was a non-event, was very important. They both had the feeling of a schoolboy after an exam — the kind that either keeps you in your class or shuts you out of school forever. Everyone present, sensing that something had taken place, talked eagerly about unrelated subjects. Levin and Kitty were particularly happy and particularly conscious of their love that evening. And their happiness in their love felt like an unintended insult to those who would have liked to feel the same and couldn't — and so the two of them felt a pang of conscience.
"Mark my words, Alexander won't come," said the old princess.
They were expecting Stepan Arkadyevitch to come down by train that evening, and the old prince had written that he might come too.
"And I know why," the princess went on. "He says young people ought to be left alone at first."
"But papa has left us alone. We never see him," said Kitty. "And besides, we're not young people anymore — we're an old married couple by now."
"If he doesn't come, I'll have to say goodbye to you children too," said the princess with a mournful sigh.
"What nonsense, mamma!" both daughters jumped on her at once.
"Think how he must be feeling. Now...."

And suddenly there was an unexpected catch in the princess's voice. Her daughters fell silent and looked at one another. "Maman always finds something to be miserable about," the glance said. They didn't know that, happy as the princess was in her daughter's house, and useful as she felt herself to be there, she had been thoroughly miserable both on her own account and on her husband's ever since they had married off their last and favorite daughter and the old home had been left empty.
"What is it, Agafea Mihalovna?" Kitty asked, suddenly turning to Agafea Mihalovna, who was standing there with a mysterious air and a face full of significance.
"About supper."
"Well, that's good," said Dolly. "You go arrange it, and I'll go hear Grisha do his lesson — otherwise he won't have done anything all day."
"That's my job! No, Dolly, I'll go," said Levin, jumping up.

Grisha, who was now in high school, had to go over the term's lessons during the summer holidays. Darya Alexandrovna, who had been doing Latin with her son in Moscow, had made it a rule, once they came to the Levins', to work through at least the hardest Latin and arithmetic with him once a day. Levin had offered to take over for her, but having once overheard one of his lessons and noticed that he wasn't going about it the way the Moscow teacher did, the mother had said firmly — though with much embarrassment, taking pains not to wound Levin — that they really had to stick strictly to the book the way the teacher had, and that she'd better take it back herself. Levin was amazed both at Stepan Arkadyevitch, who by neglecting his own duty dumped onto the mother the supervision of studies she didn't understand, and at the teachers for teaching the children so poorly. Still, he promised his sister-in-law he'd give the lessons exactly the way she wanted. And so he went on teaching Grisha, not in his own way but by the book, and consequently took little interest in it and often forgot the lesson hour. That was what had happened today.
"No, I'm going, Dolly, you stay," he said. "We'll do it all properly, just as in the book. Only when Stiva arrives and we go out shooting, then we'll have to skip it."
And Levin went off to Grisha.
Varenka was telling Kitty the same thing. Even in the Levins' happy, well-ordered household Varenka had managed to make herself useful.
"I'll see to the supper, you stay," she said, and got up to go to Agafea Mihalovna.
"Yes, yes — most likely they haven't been able to get chickens. If that's the case, ours...."
"Agafea Mihalovna and I will see about it," — and Varenka disappeared with her.
"What a nice girl!" said the princess.
"Not nice, maman — she's an exquisite girl. There's nobody else like her."

"So you're expecting Stepan Arkadyevitch today?" Sergey Ivanovitch said, plainly not inclined to keep the Varenka conversation going. "It would be hard to find two sons-in-law more different than yours," he added with a wry smile. "One all motion, living only in society, like a fish in water; the other our Kostya — lively, alert, quick at everything, but the moment he's in society he either sinks into apathy or flails around helplessly like a fish on land."

"Yes, he is very careless," the princess said, turning to Sergey Ivanovitch. "In fact, I've been meaning to ask you to tell him that there's no question of her" — she nodded at Kitty — "staying out here; she absolutely must come to Moscow. He's talking about bringing a doctor down...."
"Maman, he'll do everything; he's agreed to everything," Kitty said, angry that her mother was dragging Sergey Ivanovitch in as judge of such a matter.

In the middle of their conversation they heard horses snorting and wheels crunching on the gravel. Dolly didn't have time to get up and go meet her husband before, from the window of the room below where Grisha was having his lesson, Levin came leaping out and pulled Grisha out after him.
"It's Stiva!" Levin shouted from beneath the balcony. "We're done, Dolly, don't worry!" he added, and started off at a boy's run to meet the carriage.
"_Is ea id, ejus, ejus, ejus!_" Grisha shouted, skipping along the avenue.
"And someone else too! Papa, of course!" cried Levin, coming to a stop at the entrance to the avenue. "Kitty, don't come down the steep stairs — go around."

But Levin had been wrong to take the person in the carriage for the old prince. As he got closer he saw, sitting beside Stepan Arkadyevitch, not the prince but a handsome, stout young man in a Scotch cap with long ribbons trailing behind. This was Vassenka Veslovsky, a distant cousin of the Shtcherbatskys, a brilliant young fellow in Petersburg and Moscow society. "A capital fellow, and a passionate sportsman," as Stepan Arkadyevitch put it, introducing him.

Not in the least put off by the disappointment of arriving in place of the old prince, Veslovsky greeted Levin cheerfully, claimed acquaintance with him from years back, and, scooping Grisha up into the carriage, lifted him over the pointer Stepan Arkadyevitch had brought along.

Levin didn't climb into the carriage; he walked behind it. He was annoyed that the old prince, of whom he grew fonder the better he knew him, hadn't come, and also at the arrival of this Vassenka Veslovsky, a thoroughly uncongenial and unnecessary guest. He found him even more uncongenial and unnecessary when, approaching the steps where everyone — children and grown-ups — was gathered in excitement, Levin saw Vassenka Veslovsky, with a particularly warm and gallant air, kissing Kitty's hand.
"Your wife and I are cousins and very old friends," said Vassenka Veslovsky, shaking Levin's hand once more, very warmly.

"Well, are there plenty of birds?" Stepan Arkadyevitch said to Levin, scarcely giving anyone time to finish their greetings. "We've come down with the most savage intentions. Why, maman, they haven't been in Moscow since! Tanya, look — here's something for you. Get it, please, it's in the carriage, in the back!" he was talking in all directions at once. "How pretty you've grown, Dolly," he said to his wife, kissing her hand again, holding it in one of his and patting it with the other.
Levin, who a minute earlier had been in the happiest of moods, was now looking around darkly, and everything displeased him.
"Whose lips did those lips kiss yesterday?" he thought, watching Stepan Arkadyevitch's tender display toward his wife. He looked at Dolly, and didn't like her either.
"She doesn't believe in his love. So what is she so pleased about? Disgusting!" Levin thought.
He looked at the princess, who had been so dear to him only a minute before, and didn't like the way she was greeting this Vassenka — with all his ribbons — as though he were a fixture of the house.

Even Sergey Ivanovitch, who had come out onto the steps too, struck Levin as unpleasant in the show of cordiality he gave Stepan Arkadyevitch, even though Levin knew his brother neither liked nor respected Oblonsky.
And Varenka, even she struck him as hateful, with her _sainte nitouche_ air, getting to know this gentleman while in fact her mind was on nothing but getting married.

And more hateful than anybody was Kitty, for falling in with the tone of gaiety this gentleman set for his visit, as though the whole thing were a holiday for himself and for everyone else. And above all what was unpleasant was the particular smile with which she returned his smile.
Talking noisily, they all went into the house; but as soon as they were settled, Levin turned and walked out.

Kitty saw that something was wrong with her husband. She tried to find a moment to speak to him alone, but he made a point of getting away from her, saying he was needed at the counting-house. It had been a long time since his own work on the estate had felt so important to him as at that moment. "It's all holiday to them," he thought. "But these aren't holiday matters — they won't wait, and there's no living without them."

title: Chapter 7
paragraphs: Levin only came back to the house when they sent for him to come to supper. On the stairs Kitty and Agafea Mihalovna were standing, conferring about which wines to serve.
"But why are you making such a fuss? Serve whatever we usually have."

"No, Stiva won't drink that... Kostya, stop — what's wrong?" Kitty began, hurrying after him, but he walked straight on into the dining room without waiting for her, and immediately joined the lively conversation Vassenka Veslovsky and Stepan Arkadyevitch were keeping up there.
"Well, what do you say — are we going shooting tomorrow?" said Stepan Arkadyevitch.
"Please, let's go," said Veslovsky, shifting to another chair, where he sat down sideways with one fat leg tucked under him.

"I'd be delighted, we'll go. Have you done any shooting yet this year?" Levin said to Veslovsky, staring fixedly at his leg but speaking with that forced friendliness Kitty knew so well in him, and which was so unlike him. "I can't promise grouse, but there are plenty of snipe. Only we'll need to start early. You're not tired? Stiva, you're not tired?"
"Me, tired? I've never been tired in my life. We could stay up all night, for all I care. Let's go for a walk!"
"Yes, really, let's not go to bed at all! Wonderful!" Veslovsky chimed in.

"Oh, we all know you can go without sleep and keep other people up too," Dolly said to her husband, with that faint trace of irony that had become almost permanent in her voice when she spoke to him. "But as far as I'm concerned, it's time for bed... I'm going up, I don't want any supper."
"No, stay a little longer, Dolly," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, coming round to her side of the supper table. "I still have so much to tell you."
"Nothing important, I'm sure."
"Did you know Veslovsky has been to Anna's, and he's going back? They're hardly fifty miles from you, you know, and I really must go over there too. Veslovsky, come over here!"
Vassenka crossed over to the ladies and sat down beside Kitty.
"Tell me, please — you stayed with her? How was she?" Darya Alexandrovna asked him.

Levin was left at the other end of the table, and although he kept up his conversation with the princess and Varenka without a pause, he could see that something eager and mysterious was being discussed between Stepan Arkadyevitch, Dolly, Kitty, and Veslovsky. And that wasn't all. He saw on his wife's face a look of real feeling as she gazed, eyes fixed, at Vassenka's handsome face while he told them something with great animation.
"It's an exceptionally nice place," Veslovsky was saying about Vronsky and Anna. "I can't presume to judge, of course, but in their house you really do feel the sense of a home."
"What are they planning to do?"
"I believe they're thinking of going to Moscow."
"How splendid it would be if we all went over together! When are you going?" Stepan Arkadyevitch asked Vassenka.
"I'm spending July there."
"Will you go?" Stepan Arkadyevitch said to his wife.

"I've been wanting to for a long time, and I certainly will," said Dolly. "I feel sorry for her, and I know her. She's a splendid woman. I'll go alone, when you've gone back, and then I won't be in anyone's way. It will actually be better without you."
"Of course," said Stepan Arkadyevitch. "And you, Kitty?"
"Me? Why would I go?" Kitty said, flushing scarlet, and glanced over at her husband.
"Do you know Anna Arkadyevna, then?" Veslovsky asked her. "She's a very fascinating woman."
"Yes," she answered Veslovsky, blushing even deeper. She got up and walked over to her husband.
"So you're going shooting tomorrow?" she said.

His jealousy, in those few minutes — especially at the flush that had spread across her cheeks while she was talking to Veslovsky — had already gone a long way. Now, as he heard her words, he gave them his own twist. Strange as it seemed to him later when he looked back on it, in that instant it appeared perfectly clear to him that in asking whether he was going shooting all she really wanted to know was whether he would be giving that pleasure to Vassenka Veslovsky, with whom, he imagined, she was in love.
"Yes, I'm going," he answered her in an unnatural voice that he himself found unpleasant.
"No, better stay home tomorrow, otherwise Dolly will hardly see her husband at all, and set off the day after," said Kitty.
The motive behind Kitty's words was translated by Levin like this: "Don't separate me from _him_. I don't mind _your_ going, but do let me enjoy the company of this delightful young man."
"Oh, if you'd like, we'll stay home tomorrow," Levin answered, with peculiar friendliness.
Meanwhile Vassenka, with no idea of the misery his presence was causing, got up from the table after Kitty, and, watching her with smiling, admiring eyes, followed after her.
Levin caught that look. He went white, and for a moment he could hardly draw a breath. "How dare he look at my wife that way!" was the feeling boiling inside him.
"Tomorrow, then? Please, let's go," said Vassenka, sitting down on a chair and crossing his leg in his usual way again.

Levin's jealousy ran further still. He could already see himself as a deceived husband whom his wife and her lover regarded as nothing more than a convenient supplier of comforts and amusements... But in spite of all that, he politely and hospitably questioned Vassenka about his shooting, his gun, and his boots, and agreed to go out the next day.

Luckily for Levin, the old princess cut short his torment by standing up herself and advising Kitty to go to bed. But even now Levin could not escape another stab. As he was saying good night to his hostess, Vassenka tried once more to kiss her hand, but Kitty, reddening, pulled her hand back and said, with a naive bluntness for which the old princess scolded her afterwards:
"That isn't the way we do things."
In Levin's eyes she was at fault for having allowed such manners to take hold in the first place, and even more at fault for showing so clumsily that she didn't like them.

"How can anyone want to go to bed!" said Stepan Arkadyevitch, who, after several glasses of wine at supper, was now in his most charming and sentimental mood. "Look, Kitty," he said, pointing to the moon, which had just risen behind the lime trees, "isn't it exquisite! Veslovsky, this is the time for a serenade. You know, he has a wonderful voice — we practiced songs together along the road. He's brought some lovely songs with him, two new ones. Varvara Andreevna and he must sing some duets."
When the party had broken up, Stepan Arkadyevitch walked for a long while along the avenue with Veslovsky; their voices could be heard singing one of the new songs.

Listening to those voices, Levin sat scowling in an armchair in his wife's bedroom and kept up an obstinate silence when she asked him what was wrong. But when at last, with a timid glance, she ventured the question — "Was there perhaps something about Veslovsky you didn't like?" — it all burst out, and he told her everything. He was humiliated by what he was saying, and that infuriated him all the more.

He stood facing her, his eyes glittering menacingly under his drawn brows, his strong arms pressed across his chest as if he were straining every nerve to keep himself in check. The expression on his face would have been grim, even cruel, if it had not at the same time carried a look of suffering that touched her. His jaws were twitching, and his voice kept breaking.

"You have to understand that I am not jealous — jealousy is an ugly word. I can't be jealous, believe me... I can't say what I feel, but this is awful... I'm not jealous, but I am wounded, humiliated that anyone should dare think — that anyone should dare look at you with eyes like that."
"Eyes like what?" Kitty said, trying as scrupulously as she could to recall every word and gesture of that evening, and every nuance behind them.

At the very bottom of her heart she did think there had been something — precisely at the moment when he had crossed over after her to the other end of the table; but she didn't dare admit it even to herself, much less bring herself to say so to him and so increase his suffering.
"And what could possibly be attractive about me in the state I'm in now?..."
"Ah!" he cried, clutching his head, "you mustn't say that!... If you had been attractive then..."

"Oh no, Kostya, oh, wait — listen!" she said, looking at him with an expression of pained pity. "What can you be thinking? When for me there's no one else in the world, no one, no one!... Would you like me never to see anyone?"

For the first instant she had been offended by his jealousy; she had been angry that even the slightest amusement, even the most innocent one, should be forbidden her. But now she would gladly have sacrificed not only such trifles but everything else for his peace of mind, to spare him the agony he was going through.

"You have to understand the horror and the absurdity of my position," he went on in a desperate whisper. "That he's in my house, that strictly speaking he hasn't done anything improper apart from his free-and-easy manner and the way he sits with his legs tucked up. He thinks it's the height of style, so I'm forced to be civil to him."
"But Kostya, you're exaggerating," said Kitty, secretly rejoicing at the depth of his love for her, which was showing itself now in his jealousy.

"The most awful part of it all is that you are just as you've always been, and now especially, when for me you are something sacred, and we are so happy, so particularly happy — and all of a sudden a little wretch... He's not a little wretch; why am I abusing him? I have nothing to do with him. But why should my happiness, and yours..."
"Do you know, I understand now where it all came from," Kitty was beginning.
"Well, what? what?"
"I saw the way you looked at us while we were talking at supper."
"Well, well!" Levin said in dismay.

She told him what they had been talking about. As she told him, she was breathless with feeling. Levin was silent for a moment, then scanned her pale, distressed face, and suddenly clutched at his head.
"Katya, I've been tormenting you! Darling, forgive me! It's madness! Katya, I'm a criminal. And how could you be so upset over such an idiotic thing?"
"Oh, I was just sorry for you."
"For me? for me? How insane I am!... But why make you miserable? It's awful to think that any outsider can shatter our happiness."
"It's humiliating too, of course."
"Well then, I'll keep him here all summer and drown him in courtesy," said Levin, kissing her hands. "You'll see. Tomorrow... Oh yes, we're going tomorrow."

title: Chapter 8
paragraphs: The next day, before the ladies were up, the wagonette and a trap for the shooting party were already at the door, and Laska, who had known since early morning that they were going shooting, had whined and darted back and forth and then settled herself in the wagonette beside the coachman, where, disapproving of the delay, she watched the door intently for the sportsmen who still did not appear. The first to come out was Vassenka Veslovsky, in new high boots that reached halfway up his thick thighs, in a green blouse, with a new Russian-leather cartridge belt, and his Scottish cap with ribbons, carrying a brand-new English gun without a sling. Laska flew up to him, welcomed him, jumped up and asked him in her own way whether the others were coming soon, and when she got no answer she returned to her post and sank back into stillness, head tilted, one ear pricked to listen. At last the door opened with a creak, and Stepan Arkadyevitch's spotted-and-tan pointer Krak flew out, running in circles and turning over in the air. Stepan Arkadyevitch himself followed, gun in hand and cigar in his mouth.

"Good dog, good dog, Krak!" he called encouragingly to the dog, who had put his paws up on his chest and was snapping at his game bag. Stepan Arkadyevitch was got up in rough leggings and spats, torn trousers, and a short coat. On his head was the wreck of a hat of no particular shape, but his gun, of a new patent, was a perfect gem, and his game bag and cartridge belt, though worn, were of the very best quality.

Until now, Vassenka Veslovsky had had no idea that it was truly _chic_ for a sportsman to dress in rags while keeping his shooting equipment of the finest quality. He saw it now, looking at Stepan Arkadyevitch — radiant in his tatters, graceful, well-fed, and cheerful, the picture of a Russian gentleman. And he made up his mind that next time he went shooting he would definitely adopt the same look.
"Well, and what about our host?" he asked.
"A young wife," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, smiling.
"Yes — and such a charming one!"
"He came down already dressed. No doubt he's gone back up to her again."

Stepan Arkadyevitch had guessed correctly. Levin had run upstairs again to ask his wife one more time whether she forgave him for his idiocy the night before, and also to beg her, for Christ's sake, to be more careful. The main thing was that she keep clear of the children — they could bump into her at any moment. Then he had to hear her say once more that she was not angry with him for going away for two days, and to plead with her to send him a note by a servant on horseback the next morning, to write him even just two words, to let him know that everything was all right with her.

Kitty was upset, as she always was when she had to part with her husband for a couple of days, but when she saw his eager figure, looking big and strong in his shooting boots and white blouse, and saw a kind of hunter's elation and excitement she could not begin to share, she forgot her own dejection for the sake of his pleasure and said goodbye to him cheerfully.
"Pardon, gentlemen!" he said, running out onto the steps. "Did you put in the lunch? Why is the chestnut on the right? Well, never mind. Laska, down — go and lie down!"
"Put it in with the herd of oxen," he said to the herdsman who had been waiting for him at the steps with some question. "Excuse me, here comes another nuisance."
Levin jumped down from the wagonette, where he had already taken his seat, to meet the carpenter, who was coming toward the steps with a ruler in his hand.
"You didn't come to the office yesterday, and now you're holding me up. Well, what is it?"
"Would your honor let me put in another turn? It's only three steps to add. And we'd make it fit just right at the same time. It would be a lot more convenient."
"You should have listened to me," Levin answered with annoyance. "I said to mark the lines first and then fit the steps. Now there's no putting it right. Do as I told you, and build a new staircase."

The trouble was that in the lodge being built the carpenter had ruined the staircase by assembling it without calculating the space it had to fill, so that once it was put in place all the steps came out sloping. Now the carpenter wanted to keep the same staircase and add three more steps.
"It will work much better."
"But where is your staircase going to come out, with its three extra steps?"

"Why, upon my word, sir," the carpenter said with a contemptuous smile. "It comes out right at the right spot. It starts, so to speak," he said with a persuasive gesture, "and it comes down and comes down, and it comes out."
"But three more steps will add to the length, too... where is it going to come out?"
"Why, sure enough, it'll start from the bottom and go up and go up, and come out like so," the carpenter said, stubborn and convinced.
