"It'll hit the ceiling and the wall."
"Upon my word! It'll go up and up and come out like this."
Levin took out a ramrod and started sketching the staircase for him in the dust.
"There, do you see?"
"Whatever your honor says," the carpenter said, with a sudden flash in his eyes that showed he had finally understood. "Looks like it'll be best to build a new one."
"Well, then, do as you're told," Levin shouted, settling himself in the wagonette. "Down! Hold the dogs, Philip!"

With all his family and household worries left behind, Levin now felt such a keen sense of joy and anticipation that he was in no mood to talk. On top of that, he had that concentrated excitement every sportsman feels as he approaches the field. If anything was on his mind at the moment, it was only the question of whether they would find anything in the Kolpensky marsh, whether Laska would show to advantage next to Krak, and whether he would shoot well that day himself. Not to disgrace himself in front of a newcomer — not to be outdone by Oblonsky — that, too, crossed his mind.

Oblonsky was feeling the same and was also not talkative. Vassenka Veslovsky alone kept up a steady flow of cheerful chatter. As he listened to him now, Levin felt ashamed of how unfair he had been to him the day before. Vassenka really was a nice fellow — simple, kind-hearted, and good-humored. If Levin had met him before he was married, he would have made friends with him. Levin did rather dislike his holiday attitude to life and a certain easy assumption of elegance — as if he took it for granted that he was a person of unquestionable importance because he had long nails, a stylish cap, and so on to match. But that could be forgiven on account of his good nature and good breeding. Levin liked him for his good education, for the fact that he spoke French and English with such an excellent accent, and for being a man of his own world.

Vassenka was thoroughly delighted with the left-hand horse, which came from the Don steppes. He kept praising it enthusiastically. "How fine it must be to gallop over the steppes on a steppe horse! Don't you think?" he said. He had imagined riding a steppe horse as something wild and romantic, and it had turned out to be nothing of the kind. But his simplicity, especially combined with his good looks, his pleasant smile, and the grace of his movements, was very attractive. Whether because Vassenka's nature was congenial to him, or because Levin was trying to make up for his sins of the night before by seeing only what was good in him, he genuinely enjoyed his company.

After they had driven a couple of miles from home, Veslovsky suddenly reached for a cigar and his wallet, and could not tell whether he had lost them or left them on the table. In the wallet there were thirty-seven pounds, and so the matter could not simply be left in doubt.
"Tell you what, Levin, I'll gallop home on that left trace horse. That would be splendid. Eh?" he said, getting ready to climb down.
"No, why should you?" Levin answered, calculating that Vassenka could hardly weigh less than seventeen stone. "I'll send the coachman."
The coachman rode back on the trace horse, and Levin himself drove the remaining pair.

title: Chapter 9
paragraphs: "Well, then, what's the plan of campaign? Tell us everything," said Stepan Arkadyevitch.

"Here's the plan. Right now we're driving to Gvozdyov. At Gvozdyov, on this side, there's a grouse marsh, and on the other side of the village there are some magnificent snipe marshes, where there are also grouse. It's hot now, and we'll get there toward evening — it's about fifteen miles — and do some evening shooting; we'll spend the night there and go on tomorrow to the bigger moors."
"And there's nothing on the way?"
"Yes, but we ought to save ourselves; besides, it's hot. There are two nice little spots, but I doubt there'll be anything to shoot."

Levin would have liked to stop at those little spots himself, but they were close to home; he could shoot them any time, and they were only little places — there would barely be room for three guns. So, with a bit of dishonesty, he said he doubted there would be anything to shoot. When they reached a small marsh, Levin would have driven straight past, but Stepan Arkadyevitch, with the practiced eye of a sportsman, immediately spotted the reeds from the road.
"Shall we give it a try?" he said, pointing at the little marsh.
"Levin, please! How splendid!" Vassenka Veslovsky began begging, and Levin could only give in.
Before they even had time to stop, the dogs had flown one after the other into the marsh.
"Krak! Laska!..."
The dogs came back.

"There won't be room for three of us. I'll stay here," Levin said, hoping they would find nothing but the peewits that the dogs had startled and that were now turning in flight, wailing plaintively over the marsh.
"No! Come on, Levin, let's go together!" Veslovsky called.
"Really, there's no room. Laska, back, Laska! You don't need another dog, do you?"

Levin stayed behind with the wagonette and watched the sportsmen enviously. They walked clear across the marsh. Apart from little birds and peewits, of which Vassenka shot one, there was nothing in the marsh.
"You see now I wasn't being stingy about the marsh," Levin said, "it was just a waste of time."

"Oh no, it was great fun all the same. Did you see me?" said Vassenka Veslovsky, clambering awkwardly into the wagonette with his gun and his peewit in his hands. "How splendidly I shot that bird! Didn't I? Well, will we soon be at the real spot?"

The horses suddenly jolted forward, Levin knocked his head against the stock of someone's gun, and there was the crack of a shot. Actually the gun went off first, but to Levin it seemed the other way around. It turned out that Vassenka Veslovsky had only pulled one trigger and left the other hammer cocked. The charge flew into the ground without doing any harm. Stepan Arkadyevitch shook his head and laughed reprovingly at Veslovsky, but Levin couldn't bring himself to scold him. For one thing, any rebuke would have looked like a reaction to the danger and the bump now rising on Levin's forehead. And besides, Veslovsky was at first so naively distressed, and then laughed so good-humoredly and infectiously at the general consternation, that you couldn't help laughing with him.

When they reached the second marsh, which was fairly large and would take some time to shoot through, Levin tried to talk them out of stopping. But once again Veslovsky talked him into it. And again, since the marsh was narrow, Levin played the good host and stayed with the carriage.

Krak headed straight for some clumps of sedge. Vassenka Veslovsky was the first to run after the dog. Before Stepan Arkadyevitch had time to catch up, a grouse flew out. Veslovsky missed it, and it flew off into an unmown meadow. That grouse was now left for Veslovsky to follow up. Krak found it again and pointed, Veslovsky shot it, and then went back to the carriage. "Now you go and I'll stay with the horses," he said.
Levin had begun to feel the pangs of a sportsman's envy. He handed the reins to Veslovsky and walked into the marsh.
Laska, who had been whining piteously at the injustice of her treatment, shot straight ahead toward a promising spot Levin knew well, and that Krak had not yet covered.
"Why don't you call her back?" Stepan Arkadyevitch shouted.
"She won't scare them," Levin answered, sharing his bitch's excitement and hurrying after her.

The closer Laska got to the familiar nesting places, the more focused her searching became. A little marsh bird distracted her for no more than an instant. She made one circuit of the clump of reeds, was starting a second, and suddenly quivered with excitement and froze.

"Come on, come on, Stiva!" Levin shouted, feeling his heart starting to pound; and suddenly, as though some shutter had been thrown open inside his straining ears, every sound — confused but loud — began to beat against his hearing, all sense of distance lost. He heard Stepan Arkadyevitch's footsteps and mistook them for the distant trampling of the horses; he heard the brittle snap of twigs underfoot and took it for a grouse taking off. He also heard, not far behind him, a splashing in the water that he could not explain to himself.
Picking his way carefully, he moved up to the dog.
"Fetch it!"

Not a grouse but a snipe flew up from beside the dog. Levin had raised his gun, but at the very moment he was taking aim the splashing grew louder, came closer, and merged with the sound of Veslovsky's voice shouting something with strange loudness. Levin saw that he was pointing his gun behind the snipe, but he fired anyway.
Once he was sure he had missed, Levin looked around and saw the horses and the wagonette not on the road but out in the marsh.
Veslovsky, eager to see the shooting, had driven the horses into the marsh, and they had gotten stuck in the mud.

"Damn the fellow!" Levin muttered to himself as he walked back to the carriage sunk in the mire. "What did you drive in there for?" he said dryly to him, and called the coachman over and started hauling the horses out.

Levin was annoyed at having had his shooting interrupted, annoyed at the horses being stuck in the mud, and even more annoyed at the fact that neither Stepan Arkadyevitch nor Veslovsky was helping him and the coachman to unharness the horses and get them out, since neither of them had the faintest idea about harnessing. Without bothering to answer a syllable of Vassenka's protest that the ground had been perfectly dry there, Levin worked in silence with the coachman to get the horses free. But then, as he warmed up to the work and saw how energetically Veslovsky was tugging at the wagonette by one of the mudguards — so hard that he actually broke it — Levin reproached himself for having let yesterday's feelings make him too cold toward Veslovsky, and he tried to be especially friendly to smooth over his earlier chill. Once everything was put right and the carriage was back on the road, Levin had the lunch served.

"_Bon appétit — bonne conscience! Ce poulet va tomber jusqu'au fond de mes bottes_," quoted Vassenka, his spirits restored, as he finished his second chicken. "Well, now our troubles are over, and everything will go beautifully. Only, to atone for my sins, I'm bound to ride on the box. Right? Eh? No, no! I'll be your Automedon. You'll see how I drive you," he replied, not letting go of the rein when Levin asked him to let the coachman drive. "No, I have to atone for my sins, and I'm very comfortable on the box." And so he drove.

Levin was a little worried that he would wear the horses out, especially the chestnut, which Veslovsky did not know how to hold in; but, without realizing it, he came under the spell of his cheerfulness and listened all the way to the songs Veslovsky sang on the box, and to his descriptions and imitations of driving English-style, four-in-hand. So it was in the very best of spirits that they drove on after lunch to the Gvozdyov marsh.

title: Chapter 10
paragraphs: Vassenka drove the horses so briskly that they reached the marsh too early, while it was still hot.

As they approached this more important marsh — the main goal of their expedition — Levin couldn't help wondering how he might get rid of Vassenka and be free to move on his own. Stepan Arkadyevitch clearly had the same wish, and on his face Levin saw the look of anxiety always present in a true sportsman at the start of a shoot, together with a certain good-humored slyness that belonged to him alone.

"How shall we go about it? It's a splendid marsh, I see, and there are hawks," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, pointing at two large birds hovering over the reeds. "Where there are hawks, there's bound to be game."

"Now, gentlemen," said Levin, pulling up his boots and checking the lock of his gun with a rather gloomy expression, "do you see those reeds?" He pointed to an island of blackish green in the huge, half-mown wet meadow that stretched along the right bank of the river. "The marsh starts here, straight in front of us, you see — where it's greener? From here it runs off to the right, where the horses are; there are breeding places there, and grouse, and all around those reeds as far as that alder, and right up to the mill. Look, over there, where the pools are. That's the best spot. I once shot seventeen snipe there. We'll split up with the dogs and go in different directions, and then meet up at the mill."
"All right, who goes left and who goes right?" Stepan Arkadyevitch asked. "It's wider to the right; the two of you take that side, and I'll take the left," he added, with apparent indifference.
"Capital! We'll bring back the bigger bag! Yes, come on, come on!" Vassenka exclaimed.
Levin could only agree, and they split up.

As soon as they entered the marsh, the two dogs began to hunt together, working toward the green, slime-covered pool. Levin knew Laska's method — wary and noncommittal; he knew the spot too, and was expecting a whole covey of snipe.

"Veslovsky, walk beside me, beside me!" he said in a low voice to his companion, who was splashing in the water behind him. After that stray shot near the Kolpensky marsh, Levin couldn't help being uneasy about which way Vassenka's gun was pointed.
"Oh, I won't get in your way — don't worry about me."

But Levin couldn't help worrying, and he remembered Kitty's parting words: "Mind you don't shoot each other." The dogs were drawing closer, then passing each other, each following its own scent. The expectation of snipe was so intense that to Levin the squelch of his own heel as he dragged it up out of the mire sounded like a snipe's call, and he gripped and tightened his hand on the lock of his gun.

"Bang! Bang!" sounded almost in his ear. Vassenka had fired at a flock of ducks that was floating over the marsh and flying toward the sportsmen at that moment, far out of range. Before Levin had time to look around, there was the whir of one snipe, then another, then a third, and some eight more rose one after another.

Stepan Arkadyevitch hit one just as it was starting its zigzag flight, and the snipe dropped in a heap into the mud. Oblonsky took deliberate aim at another, still flying low over the reeds, and at the same instant as his shot that snipe too came down, and it could be seen fluttering out where the sedge had been cut, its undamaged wing showing white underneath.

Levin was not so lucky: he fired too low at his first bird and missed; he aimed at it again, just as it was rising, but at that instant another snipe flew up right at his feet, distracting him, so that he missed again.

While they were reloading their guns, another snipe rose, and Veslovsky, who had managed to reload in time, sent two charges of small shot uselessly into the water. Stepan Arkadyevitch picked up his snipe, and with sparkling eyes glanced at Levin.
"Well, let's split up now," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, and limping on his left foot, holding his gun ready and whistling to his dog, he set off in one direction. Levin and Veslovsky went in the other.

It always went the same way with Levin: when his first shots failed, he got hot and out of temper, and shot badly the rest of the day. That was how it went today. There were plenty of snipe. They kept flying up from right under the dogs, from under the sportsmen's feet, and Levin might easily have made up for his bad start. But the more he shot, the more disgraced he felt in Veslovsky's eyes, as Veslovsky kept popping away merrily and indiscriminately, hitting nothing and not in the least troubled by his lack of success. Levin, hurrying feverishly, couldn't get a grip on himself, lost his temper more and more, and ended up firing with almost no real hope of hitting anything. Even Laska seemed to grasp it. She began searching more listlessly and would glance back at the sportsmen as if with puzzlement or reproach in her eyes. Shot after shot rang out. The smoke of the powder hung around the sportsmen, and yet in the wide, roomy net of the game bag there were only three little light snipe. And of those, one had been killed by Veslovsky alone, and one by both of them together. Meanwhile, from the other side of the marsh, came the sound of Stepan Arkadyevitch's shots — not frequent, but, as Levin imagined, well aimed, since after almost each one they heard "Krak, Krak, _apporte_!"

That excited Levin all the more. The snipe were floating constantly in the air above the reeds. The whir of wings near the ground and their harsh cries higher up could be heard on every side; the snipe that had risen first and shot up into the air were settling again right in front of the sportsmen. Instead of two hawks, there were now dozens of them hovering with shrill cries over the marsh.

After walking through more than half of the marsh, Levin and Veslovsky reached the point where the peasants' hayfield was divided into long strips running down to the reeds, marked off in one place by trampled grass, in another by a path mowed through it. Half the strips had already been cut.

Though there was less hope of finding birds in the uncut part than the cut part, Levin had promised Stepan Arkadyevitch to meet him at the mill, so he kept on with his companion across the cut and uncut patches.
"Hi there, sportsmen!" shouted one of a group of peasants sitting on an unharnessed cart. "Come and have some lunch with us! Have a drop of wine!"
Levin glanced around.
"Come on, it's all right!" shouted a good-humored, bearded peasant with a red face, showing his white teeth in a grin and holding up a greenish bottle that flashed in the sun.
"_Qu'est-ce qu'ils disent_?" asked Veslovsky.

"They're inviting you to have some vodka. They've probably been dividing the meadow into lots. I'd take some," Levin said, not without a touch of guile, hoping that Veslovsky would be tempted by the vodka and go off to them.
"Why are they offering it?"
"Oh, they're celebrating. Really, you should join them. You'd find it interesting."
"_Allons, c'est curieux_."

"Go on, go on — you'll find your way to the mill!" Levin called, and looking back he was glad to see Veslovsky, bent over and stumbling with weariness, his gun held out at arm's length, making his way out of the marsh toward the peasants.
"You come too!" the peasants shouted to Levin. "Don't be shy! Try our cake!"

Levin felt a strong urge for a drop of vodka and some bread. He was exhausted, and it took a real effort to drag his unsteady legs out of the mire, and for a moment he wavered. But Laska was on point. And immediately all his weariness vanished, and he walked lightly through the swamp toward the dog. A snipe flew up at his feet; he fired and killed it. Laska was still pointing. "Fetch it!" Another bird flew up close to the dog. Levin fired. But it was a bad day for him; he missed it, and when he went to look for the one he had shot, he couldn't find that one either. He wandered all through the reeds, but Laska did not believe he had shot it, and when he sent her to find it she only pretended to hunt, without really trying. And without Vassenka there for him to blame for his failure, things didn't go any better. There were still plenty of snipe, but Levin missed one after another.

The slanting rays of the sun were still hot; his clothes, soaked through with sweat, stuck to his body; his left boot, full of water, weighed down his leg and squeaked at every step; sweat trickled down his powder-blackened face; his mouth was full of a bitter taste, his nose of the smell of powder and stagnant water; his ears rang with the constant whir of snipe; he could not touch the stock of his gun, it had grown so hot; his heart beat in short, rapid throbs; his hands trembled with excitement, and his exhausted legs stumbled and lurched over the tussocks and through the marsh — and still he walked on and still he shot. At last, after one humiliating miss, he flung his gun and his hat down on the ground.

"No, I have to get a grip on myself," he said to himself. He picked up his gun and his hat, called Laska, and walked out of the swamp. When he reached dry ground he sat down, pulled off his boot and tipped it out, then walked over to the marsh, drank some stagnant-tasting water, wetted his burning-hot gun, and washed his face and hands. Refreshed, he went back to the spot where a snipe had landed, firmly determined to stay calm.
He tried to be calm, but it was the same all over again. His finger pressed the trigger before he had really aimed. It only got worse.
He had only five birds in his game bag when he walked out of the marsh toward the alders where he was to rejoin Stepan Arkadyevitch.

Before he caught sight of Stepan Arkadyevitch he spotted his dog. Krak shot out from behind the twisted root of an alder, black all over with the stinking mire of the marsh, and with the air of a victor sniffed at Laska. Behind Krak the well-built figure of Stepan Arkadyevitch came into view in the shade of the alder. He walked toward Levin, red and sweating, his collar unbuttoned, still limping in the same way.
"Well? You've been blazing away!" he said, smiling good-humoredly.
"And how did you do?" Levin asked. But there was no need to ask — he had already seen the full game bag.
"Oh, pretty fair."
He had fourteen birds.
"A splendid marsh! No doubt Veslovsky got in your way. It's awkward shooting with just one dog, too," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, to soften his triumph.

title: Chapter 11
paragraphs: When Levin and Stepan Arkadyevitch reached the peasant's hut where Levin always stayed, Veslovsky was already there. He was sitting in the middle of the room, gripping the bench with both hands while a soldier — the peasant's wife's brother — pulled him along by his mud-caked boots, trying to get them off. Veslovsky was laughing his infectious, good-humored laugh.

"I've only just gotten in. _Ils ont été charmants_. Just imagine — they gave me drink, fed me! Such bread, it was exquisite! _Délicieux!_ And the vodka, I never tasted any better. And they wouldn't take a penny for any of it. And they kept saying, 'Excuse our homely ways.'"

"What would they take anything for? They were treating you as a guest, of course. Do you suppose they keep vodka for sale?" the soldier said, finally getting the soaked boot off the blackened stocking.

In spite of the filth of the hut, all muddied by their boots and the dirty dogs licking themselves clean, and the smell of marsh slime and powder that filled the room, and the lack of knives and forks, the party drank their tea and ate their supper with a relish known only to sportsmen. Washed and clean, they then went into a hay barn that had been swept ready for them, where the coachman had been making up beds for the gentlemen.
Although it was already dusk, none of them wanted to go to sleep.

After drifting through reminiscences and anecdotes about guns, dogs, and former shooting parties, the conversation settled on a topic that interested all three of them. After Vassenka had several times expressed his admiration for this delightful sleeping place among the fragrant hay, this delightful broken cart (he had assumed it was broken because the shafts had been taken off), the good nature of the peasants who had treated him to vodka, and the dogs lying at their respective masters' feet, Oblonsky began telling them about a delightful shooting party at Malthus's that he had attended the previous summer.

Malthus was a well-known capitalist who had made his money speculating in railway shares. Stepan Arkadyevitch described what grouse moors this Malthus had bought up in the Tver province, how they were preserved, the carriages and dogcarts in which the shooting party had been driven about, and the luncheon pavilion that had been rigged up by the marsh.

"I don't understand you," said Levin, sitting up in the hay. "How is it that men like that don't disgust you? I can see that a lunch with Lafitte is all very pleasant, but don't you find that very lavishness distasteful? All those men, just like the old spirit monopolists in our day, make their money in a way that earns them everyone's contempt. They don't care about that contempt, and then they use their dishonest gains to buy off the contempt they have earned."
"Perfectly true!" chimed in Vassenka Veslovsky. "Perfectly! Oblonsky goes, of course, out of _bonhomie_, but other people say, 'Well, if Oblonsky stays with them...'"

"Not a bit of it." Levin could hear from Oblonsky's voice that he was smiling as he spoke. "I simply don't regard him as any more dishonest than any other rich merchant or aristocrat. They've all made their money in the same way — through their work and their intelligence."
"Oh, what kind of work? Do you call it work to get hold of concessions and then speculate with them?"
"Of course it's work. Work in the sense that if it weren't for him and others like him, there wouldn't be any railways."
"But it isn't work the way a peasant's work is work, or a scholar's."
"Granted, but it's work in the sense that his activity produces a result — the railways. Though of course you think railways are useless."
"No, that's a separate question; I'm willing to grant they're useful. But any profit that's out of all proportion to the labor that went into it is dishonest."
"But who's to say what's proportionate?"

"Profit made by dishonest means — by trickery," said Levin, aware that he could not draw a clean line between honesty and dishonesty. "Banking, for example," he went on. "It's an evil — the piling up of huge fortunes without labor, exactly the same thing as the old spirit monopolies; only the form has changed. _Le roi est mort, vive le roi_. No sooner had the spirit monopolies been abolished than along came the railways and the banking houses; that, too, is profit without work."

"Yes, that may all be very true and clever... Lie down, Krak!" Stepan Arkadyevitch called to his dog, who was scratching and turning over all the hay. He was clearly sure he was right, and so spoke calmly and without hurry. "But you haven't drawn the line between honest and dishonest work. The fact that I receive a bigger salary than my chief clerk, though he knows more about the work than I do — is that dishonest, in your view?"
"I can't say."

"Well, I'll tell you something: the fact that you receive, let's say, five thousand for your work on the land, while our host, the peasant here, no matter how hard he works, can never get more than fifty roubles, is just as dishonest as my earning more than my chief clerk, or Malthus's earning more than a stationmaster. No, on the contrary — I see that society takes a kind of hostile attitude toward these men, and it has no basis whatever; I suspect there's envy at the bottom of it..."
"No, that's not fair," said Veslovsky; "how can envy come into it? There's just something not right about that kind of business."
"You say," Levin went on, "that it's unjust for me to receive five thousand while the peasant gets fifty; that's true. It is unfair, and I feel it, but..."

"It really is. Why do we spend our days riding around, drinking, shooting, doing nothing, while they're always at work?" Vassenka Veslovsky said, evidently thinking the question through for the first time in his life and therefore considering it in perfect sincerity.
"Yes, you feel it, but you don't give him your property," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, deliberately, it seemed, to provoke Levin.

Lately a kind of quiet antagonism had grown up between the two brothers-in-law — as if, having married sisters, a sort of rivalry had sprung up between them over which of them was running his life better, and now that hostility was beginning to show in the conversation, which was taking on a personal edge.
"I don't give it away because nobody asks me to, and even if I wanted to, I couldn't give it away," Levin answered, "and I'd have no one to give it to."
"Give it to this peasant, he wouldn't say no."
"Yes, but how am I supposed to give it up? Am I to go to him and draw up a deed of conveyance?"
"I don't know; but if you're convinced you have no right to it..."
"I'm not at all convinced of that. On the contrary, I feel that I have no right to give it up — that I have duties both to the land and to my family."
"No, excuse me — if you think this inequality is unjust, why don't you act on it?..."
"Well, I do act on it negatively, in the sense that I don't try to widen the gap between him and me."
"No, excuse me, but that's a paradox."

"Yes, there's something of a sophistry about that," Veslovsky agreed. "Ah! our host — so you're not asleep yet?" he said to the peasant, who came into the barn just then, opening the creaking door. "How is it you're not asleep?"

"No, how could anyone sleep! I thought you gentlemen would be asleep already, but I heard you chattering. I came to get a hook from here. She won't bite?" he added, stepping cautiously in his bare feet.
"And where will you sleep?"
"We're going out for the night with the cattle."

"Ah, what a night!" said Veslovsky, looking out past the edge of the hut at the unharnessed wagonette, just visible in the faint light of the evening glow, framed by the open doors. "But listen — there are women's voices singing, and, my word, not badly either. Who's that singing, my friend?"
"That's the maids from just over there."
"Let's go, let's take a walk! We're not going to sleep anyway. Oblonsky, come on!"
"If only one could do both — lie here and go," Oblonsky answered, stretching. "It's wonderful lying here."

"Well, I'll go on my own then," said Veslovsky, getting up eagerly and pulling on his shoes and stockings. "Goodbye, gentlemen. If it's any fun, I'll come back for you. You've shown me some good sport, and I won't forget you."
"He really is a fine fellow, isn't he?" Stepan Arkadyevitch said when Veslovsky had gone out and the peasant had closed the door behind him.

"Yes, fine," Levin answered, still turning over the subject of their conversation in his mind. It seemed to him that he had spelled out his thoughts and feelings as clearly as he could, and yet both of these straightforward, no-fool men had said in the same breath that he was comforting himself with sophistries. That troubled him.

"It's just this, my dear boy. You have to do one of two things: either admit that the current order of society is just, and then defend your rights within it; or admit that you're enjoying unjust privileges, the way I do, and then enjoy them and be satisfied."
"No — if it were unjust, you couldn't enjoy those privileges and feel content; I at least couldn't. The main thing for me is to feel that I'm not to blame."
"What do you say, why don't we go after all?" said Stepan Arkadyevitch, evidently tired of the strain of thinking. "We're not going to sleep, you know. Come on, let's go!"

Levin didn't answer. What they had said in the conversation — that he was being just only in a negative sense — kept turning in his mind. "Can it really be that one can only be just negatively?" he was asking himself.

"How strong the smell of the fresh hay is, though," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, getting up. "There's no chance of sleeping. Vassenka has been kicking up some fun out there. Do you hear the laughter, and his voice? Hadn't we better go? Come on!"
"No, I'm not coming," Levin answered.
"Surely that's not a matter of principle, too," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, smiling, as he felt around in the dark for his cap.
"It's not a matter of principle, but why should I go?"
"You know you're storing up trouble for yourself," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, finding his cap and standing up.
"How so?"

"Do you think I haven't seen the line you've taken with your wife? I heard how it became a matter of the greatest importance whether you were to go away for a couple of days' shooting or not. That's all very well as a charming little episode, but as a rule for your whole life it won't do. A man has to be independent; he has his own masculine interests. A man has to be manly," said Oblonsky, opening the door.
"In what way? By chasing after servant girls?" said Levin.

"Why not, if it amuses him? _Ça ne tire pas à conséquence_. It does my wife no harm and it gives me a bit of fun. The main thing is to respect the sanctity of home. Nothing of the sort goes on at home. But don't tie your own hands."
"Perhaps," said Levin dryly, and he turned over on his side. "Tomorrow morning, early, I want to go shooting, and I won't wake anyone, and I'll be off at daybreak."

"_Messieurs, venez vite!_" they heard Veslovsky's voice coming back. "_Charmante!_ I've made such a discovery. _Charmante!_ A perfect Gretchen, and I've already made friends with her. Really, exceedingly pretty," he announced approvingly, as if she had been made pretty entirely for his benefit and he was now expressing his satisfaction with the entertainment provided for him.
Levin pretended to be asleep, while Oblonsky, putting on his slippers and lighting a cigar, walked out of the barn, and before long their voices died away.

For a long time Levin could not get to sleep. He heard the horses munching hay, then heard the peasant and his eldest boy getting ready and going out for the night watch with the cattle, then heard the soldier settling down on the other side of the barn with his nephew, the host's younger son. He heard the boy in his small, shrill voice telling his uncle what he thought about the dogs, who looked enormous and terrifying to him, asking what the dogs were going to hunt the next day, and the soldier answering in a hoarse, sleepy voice that the gentlemen were going to the marsh in the morning to shoot with their guns. Then, to put a stop to the boy's questions, he said, "Go to sleep, Vaska — go to sleep, or you'll catch it," and soon he himself began to snore, and everything fell still. He could hear only the snorting of the horses and the throaty cry of a snipe.
"Is it really only negative?" he repeated to himself. "Well, what of it? It isn't my fault." And he began thinking about the next day.

"Tomorrow I'll go out early, and I'll make a point of keeping cool. There are plenty of snipe, and grouse too. When I get back, there'll be the note from Kitty. Yes, Stiva may be right — I'm not manly with her, I'm tied to her apron strings... Well, it can't be helped! Negative again..."

Half asleep, he caught the laughter and the cheerful chatter of Veslovsky and Stepan Arkadyevitch. For a moment he opened his eyes: the moon was up, and in the doorway, brightly lit by the moonlight, the two of them were standing and talking. Stepan Arkadyevitch was saying something about the freshness of one of the girls, comparing her to a freshly peeled nut, and Veslovsky with his infectious laugh was repeating some line, probably said to him by a peasant: "Ah, you do your best to get round her!" Levin, half asleep, said:
"Gentlemen, tomorrow before dawn!" and fell asleep.

title: Chapter 12
paragraphs: Waking at first light, Levin tried to rouse his companions. Vassenka was face down with one stockinged leg sticking out, asleep so deeply that no nudging got a response. Oblonsky, half conscious, refused to get up at that hour. Even Laska, curled into the hay, came to her feet reluctantly, then stretched and straightened her hind legs one after the other. Levin pulled on his stockings and boots, took his gun, eased the creaking barn door open, and stepped out into the road. The coachmen were asleep in their carriages, the horses were dozing. Only one of them was still chewing oats, its nose down in the manger. Outside, everything was still gray.
"Up so early, my dear?" said the old woman who was their hostess, coming out of the hut and speaking to him with the warmth of an old friend.
"Going shooting, granny. Is this the way to the marsh?"

"Straight out the back, dear — past our threshing floor and the hemp patches. There's a little footpath." Stepping carefully on her sunburnt bare feet, the old woman led Levin out and moved the fence aside for him by the threshing floor.
"Straight on and you'll come to the marsh. Our boys took the cattle out there last night."

Laska ran eagerly ahead along the little path. Levin followed at a brisk, light pace, glancing constantly at the sky. He hoped to reach the marsh before the sun was up. But the sun was not waiting. The moon, which had been bright when he set out, was now only a curve of quicksilver. The pink wash of dawn that had been impossible to miss earlier now had to be hunted for to be seen at all. What had been only vague blurs in the distance were now sharp and distinct. They were sheaves of rye. The dew, invisible until the sun rose, soaked Levin's legs and his shirt above the belt as he passed through the tall, fragrant hemp patch, where the pollen had already dropped. In the clean stillness of the morning every small sound carried. A bee shot past his ear with the whine of a bullet. He looked carefully and saw a second, then a third. They were all flying out from the hives behind the hedge and disappearing across the hemp patch in the direction of the marsh. The path went straight to it. He could pick the marsh out by the mist over it — thicker in some places, thinner in others — so that the reeds and willow clumps stood up like islands in the haze. Along the edge of the marsh, between it and the road, peasant boys and men who had been minding the horses overnight lay asleep under their coats in the half-light. A short way off three horses stood hobbled. One of them rattled a chain. Laska walked beside her master, pressing a little ahead, looking around. Past the sleeping peasants and at the first stand of reeds, Levin checked his pistols and let the dog go. One of the horses, a sleek dark-brown three-year-old, caught sight of the dog, shied, swished its tail and snorted. The other horses were spooked too, and they splashed through the water on their hobbled legs, dragging their hoofs out of the deep mud with a squelching sound as they crashed out of the marsh. Laska stopped, gave the horses an ironic look and her master a questioning one. He patted her and whistled to signal that she could start.
Laska bounded happily and nervously through the bog as it gave way under her.

Pushing into the marsh, in among the familiar smells of roots, marsh plants, and slime, with the foreign smell of horse dung mixed in, Laska picked up at once the scent that ran through the whole marsh — the strong scent of that bird that always excited her more than any other. Here and there, among the moss and the marsh growth, the scent was very strong, but it was impossible to tell from any one spot in which direction it grew stronger or weaker. To work out the direction she had to get farther downwind. Without feeling her legs under her, Laska sprang forward in stiff bounds — bounds short enough that she could stop dead at any of them — moving to the right, against the wind blowing in from the east before sunrise, and turned to face it. Sniffing the air with her nostrils wide, she knew right away that not only the tracks but the birds themselves were just ahead of her, and more than one. Laska slowed. They were here, but where exactly she still could not say. To pin down the spot she began circling, and just then her master's voice pulled her off. "Laska! here?" he called, pointing her toward a different direction. She stopped and asked him whether she might not be better off going on the way she had begun. But he repeated his command sharply, pointing to a patch of standing water where there could not possibly be anything. She did as he said, pretending to search to keep him happy, went around it, came back to her old position, and at once had the scent again. Now that he was no longer interfering she knew what to do, and without watching her feet — to her annoyance she stumbled over a tall stump into the water but righted herself with her strong, supple legs — she began the circle that would make everything clear to her. The scent grew on her, stronger and stronger, more and more defined, and all at once she knew with absolute certainty that one of them was right there, behind this tuft of reeds, five paces in front of her. She stopped, and her whole body went still and rigid. On her short legs she could not see anything ahead, but by the scent she knew it was sitting no more than five paces away. She stood, more and more aware of it, savoring it in anticipation. Her tail was stretched out tense and straight, only the tip of it twitching. Her mouth was slightly open, her ears up. One ear had folded back the wrong way as she ran in, and she was breathing hard but carefully, watching, still more carefully — more with her eyes than by turning her head — for her master. He was coming with the face she knew so well, though the eyes were always frightening to her. He stumbled over the stump as he came, and to her mind he was moving extraordinarily slowly. She thought he was crawling, but he was running.

Catching the way Laska had crouched, almost flattening to the ground, scraping deep prints with her hind paws, her mouth slightly open, Levin knew she was pointing at grouse, and with a silent prayer for luck — especially on the first bird — he ran up to her. When he came right up to her, he could, from his height, see beyond her, and he saw with his eyes what she was reading with her nose. In a gap between two little thickets, only a couple of yards away, he could see a grouse. It had turned its head and was listening. Then, with a quick preen and a folding of its wings, it slipped around a corner with an awkward flick of its tail.
"Fetch it, fetch it!" Levin shouted, giving Laska a shove from behind.

"But I can't go," Laska was thinking. "Where am I to go? From here I can feel them, but if I move forward I won't know where they are or who they are." But then he gave her a push with his knee and said in an excited whisper, "Fetch it, Laska."

"Well, if that's what he wants, I'll do it, but I can't answer for what happens now," she thought, and she shot forward as fast as her legs could carry her through the thick bushes. She had lost the scent now; she could only see and hear, and she understood nothing.

Ten paces from where she had been, a grouse rose with a guttural cry and the peculiar round whir of its wings. The instant the shot came, it dropped heavily, its white breast hitting the wet mire. A second bird did not wait — it broke behind Levin without the dog. By the time he turned, it was already some way off. But his shot caught it. After flying twenty paces farther, that second grouse pitched upward, spun in the air like a ball, and dropped heavily on a patch of dry ground.
"Now this is going to be something!" thought Levin, packing the warm, plump grouse into his game bag. "Eh, Laska — is it going to be a good day?"

When Levin had reloaded and moved on, the sun was fully up, though hidden behind storm clouds. The moon had lost all its sheen and hung in the sky like a white cloud. Not a single star was left. The sedge, which had been silver with dew, now shone like gold. The standing pools all looked like amber. The blue cast of the grass had turned to a yellow-green. Marsh birds twittered and swarmed around the brook and on the bushes, which sparkled with dew and threw long shadows. A hawk woke, settled on a haycock, turned its head this way and that, and looked at the marsh as if it disapproved. Crows wheeled across the field, and a barefoot boy was driving the horses to an old man who had risen from under his long coat and was combing his hair. The smoke from the gun lay over the green grass as white as milk.
One of the boys ran up to Levin.
"Uncle, there were ducks here yesterday!" he called, and walked along a little way behind him.
And it gave Levin double pleasure, in front of this boy who was so impressed, to bring down three snipe in a row.

title: Chapter 13
paragraphs: The hunter's old saying — that if the first beast or the first bird isn't missed, the day will be lucky — turned out to be right.

By ten o'clock Levin, tired, hungry, and happy after a twenty-mile tramp, came back to where they had spent the night with nineteen pieces of fine game and one duck, which he had tied to his belt because it would not fit in the bag. His companions had been awake a long time and had had time to get hungry and eat breakfast.

"Wait, wait, I know there are nineteen," said Levin, counting through the grouse and snipe a second time — they looked so much less impressive now, bent and dried and bloodied, their heads twisted to one side, than they had when they were flying.
The count was confirmed, and Stepan Arkadyevitch's envy pleased Levin. He was pleased too to find, when he got back, that the man Kitty had sent with a note was already there.

"I am perfectly well and happy. If you were worried about me, you can stop worrying altogether. I've got a new bodyguard, Marya Vlasyevna," — this was the midwife, a new and important figure in Levin's household — "she has come to take a look at me. She found me perfectly well, and we have kept her on until you get back. Everyone is happy and well, and please, don't hurry home — if the shooting is good, stay another day."

These two pleasures — his lucky day and the letter from his wife — were so great that two slightly unpleasant incidents passed over Levin lightly. The first was that the chestnut trace horse, plainly overworked the day before, was off his feed and looked miserable. The coachman said the horse had been "overdriven yesterday, Konstantin Dmitrievitch. That he was! Ten miles run with no sense at all!"

The other annoyance, which spoiled his mood for the first minute though he laughed about it long afterward, was discovering that of all the provisions Kitty had packed in such abundance — enough, you'd have thought, for a week — there was nothing left. On the way back, tired and hungry from shooting, Levin had had such a vivid mental picture of meat pies that as he came up to the hut he was practically smelling and tasting them the way Laska had smelt the game, and he immediately told Philip to bring some out. It turned out there were no pies left — not even any chicken.
"What an appetite this fellow has!" said Stepan Arkadyevitch, laughing and pointing at Vassenka Veslovsky. "I never have trouble eating, but he's something extraordinary!..."
"Well, can't be helped," said Levin, looking at Veslovsky bleakly. "All right, Philip, give me some beef, then."
"The beef's been eaten, and the bones given to the dogs," answered Philip.
Levin was so put out that he said, in a hurt voice, "You might have left me something!" and he felt close to tears.
"Put the game away," he said in a shaky voice to Philip, trying not to look at Vassenka, "and cover it with some nettles. And could you at least ask for some milk for me?"
But once he had drunk some milk he was instantly ashamed of having let a stranger see his irritation, and he began laughing at his own hungry misery.
In the evening they went shooting again, Veslovsky had several good shots, and that night they drove home.

The drive back was as lively as the drive out had been. Veslovsky sang songs and recounted with relish his adventures with the peasants, who had plied him with vodka and told him, "Forgive our rough ways," and his nighttime adventures with kiss-in-the-ring and the servant girl and the peasant who had asked whether he was married, and on hearing that he was not, had told him, "Now, mind you don't go chasing other men's wives — better get one of your own." That line had especially delighted Veslovsky.
"All in all, I've had a splendid time on this trip. And you, Levin?"

"So have I, very much," Levin said, and he meant it. He was particularly glad to be free of the hostility he had felt toward Vassenka Veslovsky at home, and to feel instead the friendliest disposition toward him.

title: Chapter 14
paragraphs: Next day at ten o'clock Levin, who had already done his rounds, knocked at the room where Vassenka had been put up for the night.
"_Entrez!_" Veslovsky called to him. "Forgive me, I've just finished washing," he said, smiling, standing in front of him in nothing but his underclothes.
"Don't worry about me." Levin sat down by the window. "Did you sleep well?"
"Like the dead. What's the day like for shooting?"
"What will you have — tea or coffee?"
"Neither. I'll wait for lunch. I'm really ashamed of myself. The ladies must be downstairs by now? A walk just now would be perfect. You can show me your horses."

After they had walked through the garden, looked in at the stable, and even done some gymnastics together on the parallel bars, Levin came back to the house with his guest and went with him into the drawing room.
"We had splendid shooting, and so many marvelous things happened!" Veslovsky was saying, going up to Kitty, who was sitting at the samovar. "What a shame ladies are shut out of all this!"

"Well, I suppose he has to say something to the lady of the house," Levin told himself. Once again he thought he caught something in the smile, in the conquering air with which their guest addressed Kitty....

The princess, sitting on the other side of the table with Marya Vlasyevna and Stepan Arkadyevitch, called Levin over and started talking to him about moving to Moscow for Kitty's confinement, and about preparing rooms. Just as Levin had hated all the petty preparations for his wedding, as somehow beneath the grandeur of the event, now he found the preparations for the coming birth even more offensive — the way they were counting the date, it seemed, on their fingers. He tried to shut his ears to these discussions of what patterns of long clothes were best for the coming baby; tried to turn away and avoid the sight of the mysterious, endless strips of knitting, the little linen triangles, and all the rest of it to which Dolly attached such importance. The birth of a son (he was certain it would be a son), which had been promised him but which he still could not believe in — it seemed too miraculous — presented itself in his mind on one side as a happiness so enormous and therefore so unbelievable, and on the other as something so mysterious that this assumption of definite knowledge of what would happen, and the corresponding preparation for it as if it were one of those ordinary events that happen to people, struck him as confusing and humiliating.

But the princess did not understand any of this and put his unwillingness to think and talk about it down to carelessness and indifference, so she gave him no peace. She had asked Stepan Arkadyevitch to look at a flat, and now she summoned Levin over.
"I know nothing about it, princess. Do as you think best," he said.
"You'll have to decide when you'll move."
"I really don't know. I know that millions of children are born away from Moscow, with doctors ... well...."
"But if that's how...."
"Oh, whatever Kitty wants."
"We can't talk to Kitty about it! Do you want me to frighten her? Just this spring Natalia Golitzina died because she had an incompetent doctor."
"I'll do exactly as you say," he said gloomily.

The princess went on talking, but he wasn't listening. The conversation with the princess had grated on him, but that wasn't really why he was so dark. What was bothering him was what he was seeing at the samovar.
"No, it's impossible," he thought, glancing now and then at Vassenka leaning over Kitty, telling her something with his charming smile, and at her — flushed and shaken.

There was something not nice in Vassenka's posture, in his eyes, in his smile. And Levin even saw something not nice in Kitty's posture and look as well. And again the light went out of his eyes. Again, just as before, with no warning at all, he felt himself flung down from a height of happiness, peace, and dignity into a pit of despair, rage, and humiliation. Once more everyone and everything had become hateful to him.
"Whatever you think best, princess," he said again, looking around.
"Heavy is the cap of Monomach," Stepan Arkadyevitch said playfully, hinting clearly not just at the conversation with the princess but at the cause of Levin's agitation, which he had spotted.
"How late you are today, Dolly!"

Everyone got up to greet Darya Alexandrovna. Vassenka rose only for a second, and with the rudeness toward women that the modern young man specializes in, barely bowed and went back to his conversation, laughing at something.
"I've been worried about Masha. She didn't sleep well, and she's been impossible today," said Dolly.

The conversation Vassenka had started with Kitty was running along the same lines as the evening before — about Anna, and about whether love should be placed higher than worldly considerations. Kitty disliked the subject, and was uncomfortable both with what was being said and the tone in which it was being said, and also because she knew exactly what effect it was having on her husband. But she was too simple and innocent to know how to cut the conversation short, or even to hide the surface pleasure she got from the young man's very obvious admiration. She wanted to stop it but didn't know how. Whatever she did, she knew her husband would see it and put the worst possible reading on it. And in fact, when she asked Dolly what was the matter with Masha, and Vassenka, waiting for this dull interruption to be over, started looking blankly at Dolly, the question struck Levin as an unnatural, sickening piece of hypocrisy.
"What do you say — shall we go looking for mushrooms today?" said Dolly.

"By all means, yes — and I'll come too," said Kitty, and she blushed. Out of politeness she wanted to ask Vassenka whether he would come, but she didn't ask him. "Where are you off to, Kostya?" she asked her husband, with a guilty face, as he walked past her with a determined step. That guilty look confirmed every one of his suspicions.
"The mechanic came while I was out — I haven't seen him yet," he said, not looking at her.
He went downstairs, but before he had even left his study he heard his wife's familiar footsteps running headlong after him.
"What do you want?" he said to her shortly. "We're busy."
"I beg your pardon," she said to the German mechanic; "I'd like a word with my husband."
The German started to leave the room, but Levin said to him:
"Don't trouble yourself."
"The train is at three?" the German asked. "I mustn't be late."
Levin didn't answer him; he walked out himself with his wife.
"Well, what is it you want to say to me?" he said to her in French.
He didn't look her in the face, and he didn't care to see that in her condition she was trembling all over, and her face was wretched and crushed.
"I ... I want to say that we can't go on like this, that this is misery...." she said.
"The servants are right there at the sideboard," he said angrily; "don't make a scene."
"Well, let's go in here, then!"
They were standing in the corridor. Kitty would have gone into the next room, but in there the English governess was giving Tanya a lesson.
"All right, come into the garden."

In the garden they ran into a peasant weeding the path. And by now no longer caring that the peasant could see her tear-stained face and his agitated one, that they looked like people running from some catastrophe, they went on with quick steps, feeling they had to speak it out and clear up whatever lay between them, that they had to be alone together so they could put an end to the misery they were both in.
"We can't go on like this! It's misery! I am wretched, you are wretched. What for?" she said, when they had at last reached an isolated garden bench at a bend in the lime tree avenue.

"But tell me one thing — was there in his tone anything unseemly, anything not right, anything humiliating, anything horrible?" he said, standing in front of her again in the same posture, with his clenched fists against his chest, the way he had stood that night.

"Yes," she said in a shaking voice; "but, Kostya, surely you can see I'm not to blame? All morning I've been trying to set a different tone ... but with people like that.... Why did he have to come? How happy we were!" she said, breathless with the sobs that shook her.

Although nothing was chasing them, and there was nothing to flee from, and there could not possibly have been anything especially delightful on that garden bench, the gardener was astonished to see that as they walked back past him on their way home, their faces were calm and shining.

title: Chapter 15
paragraphs: After taking his wife upstairs, Levin went to Dolly's part of the house. Darya Alexandrovna was also having a difficult day. She was walking around the room, talking sharply to a little girl who stood roaring in the corner.

"And you shall stand all day in the corner, and have your dinner all by yourself, and not see a single one of your dolls, and I won't make you a new frock," she was saying, at her wits' end how to punish her.
"Oh, she is a horrible child!" she said, turning to Levin. "Where does she pick up such wicked instincts?"
"Why, what's she done?" Levin asked without much interest, for he had come to ask her advice and was annoyed at having arrived at a bad moment.

"Grisha and she went into the raspberries, and there ... I really can't tell you what she did. It's a great pity Miss Elliot isn't with us anymore. This one watches nothing — she's a machine.... _Figurez-vous que la petite_?..."
And Darya Alexandrovna described Masha's crime.
"That proves nothing — it's not a question of wicked instincts at all, it's pure mischief," Levin assured her.
"But something has upset you? What have you come for?" Dolly asked. "What's going on in there?"
And from the tone of her question Levin felt that it would be easy to tell her what he had come to say.
"I wasn't with them — I've been alone in the garden with Kitty. We've had a quarrel for the second time since ... Stiva arrived."
Dolly looked at him with her shrewd, understanding eyes.
"Come, tell me honestly — was there in that gentleman's manner, not in Kitty's, but his, a tone that might be unpleasant — not unpleasant, but horrible, insulting, to a husband?"

"You mean — how shall I put it.... Stay there, stay in the corner!" she said to Masha, who had detected a faint smile on her mother's face and had started to turn around. "The world's verdict would be that he is behaving the way young men behave. _Il fait la cour à une jeune et jolie femme_, and a husband who is a man of the world should only be flattered by it."
"Yes, yes," Levin said gloomily; "but did you notice it?"
"Not only I — Stiva noticed it too. Right after breakfast he said to me in exactly those words: _Je crois que Veslovsky fait un petit brin de cour à Kitty_."
"Well, that settles it. Now I'm satisfied. I'll send him away," said Levin.

"What are you talking about? Have you lost your mind?" Dolly cried, horrified. "Nonsense, Kostya — just think about it!" she said, laughing. "You can go to Fanny now," she said to Masha. "No — if you really want it, I'll talk to Stiva. He'll take him away. He can say you're expecting visitors. He doesn't belong in the house anyway."
"No, no, I'll do it myself."
"But you'll have a row with him?"

"Not at all. I'll enjoy it," said Levin, his eyes flashing with real pleasure. "Come, forgive her, Dolly — she won't do it again," he said about the little sinner, who hadn't gone to Fanny but was standing uncertainly in front of her mother, waiting and looking up from under her brows to catch her mother's eye.
The mother looked at her. The child burst into sobs and hid her face in her mother's lap, and Dolly laid her thin, gentle hand on the child's head.
"And what is there in common between us and him?" thought Levin, and he went off to find Veslovsky.
As he passed through the corridor he gave orders for the carriage to be made ready for a drive to the station.
"The spring broke yesterday," said the footman.
"The covered trap, then — and quickly. Where's our visitor?"
"The gentleman has gone up to his room."
Levin caught Veslovsky just as the man had unpacked his things from his trunk, laid out some new sheet music, and was putting on his gaiters to go out riding.

Whether there was something out of the ordinary in Levin's face, or because Vassenka himself sensed that _ce petit brin de cour_ he had been making was out of place in this household, he was a little (as much as a young man in society can be) thrown by Levin's coming in.
"You ride in gaiters?"
"Yes, it's much cleaner," said Vassenka, putting his stout leg on a chair, fastening the lower hook, smiling with simple-hearted good humor.
He was clearly a good-natured fellow, and Levin, his host, felt sorry for him and ashamed of himself when he saw the shy look on Vassenka's face.

On the table lay a piece of stick that they had broken together that morning testing their strength against each other. Levin picked up the fragment and started smashing it up, snapping bits off the stick, not knowing how to begin.
"I wanted...." He stopped, but then suddenly, remembering Kitty and everything that had happened, he said, looking him squarely in the face: "I've given orders for the horses to be put-to for you."
"What for?" Vassenka began in surprise. "To drive where?"
"For you to drive to the station," Levin said grimly.
"Are you leaving — or has something happened?"

"It happens I'm expecting visitors," said Levin, his strong fingers snapping off the split ends of the stick faster and faster. "And I'm not expecting visitors, and nothing has happened, but I'm asking you to leave. Take my rudeness whatever way you like."
Vassenka drew himself up.
"I'd like an explanation...." he said with dignity, finally getting it.
"I can't explain it," Levin said quietly and deliberately, trying to keep his jaw from trembling; "and you'd be better off not asking."
And when the split ends were all gone, Levin gripped the thick ends in his fingers, snapped the stick in two, and carefully caught the falling piece.

Probably it was the sight of those tense fingers, of the muscles he had seen in action at gymnastics that morning, of the glittering eyes, the soft voice, and the trembling jaw that convinced Vassenka better than any words could. He bowed, shrugged, and smiled scornfully.
"Could I not see Oblonsky?"
The shrug and the smile did not irritate Levin.
"What else was there for him to do?" he thought.
"I'll send him to you right away."

"What sort of madness is this?" Stepan Arkadyevitch said when, after hearing from his friend that he was being thrown out of the house, he found Levin in the garden, where he was walking around waiting for his guest to leave. "_Mais c'est ridicule!_ What fly has stung you? _Mais c'est du dernier ridicule!_ What were you thinking — that just because a young man...."
But the spot where Levin had been stung was clearly still raw — he went pale again as Stepan Arkadyevitch tried to expand on the matter, and he cut him off himself.

"Please don't go into it! I can't help it. I'm ashamed of how I'm treating you and him. But I don't suppose his leaving will be any great sorrow to him, and his presence had become distasteful to me and to my wife."
"But it's an insult to him! _Et puis c'est ridicule_."
"It's both an insult and distressing to me too! And I'm not at fault in any way, and there's no reason I should suffer."
"Well, I really didn't expect this from you! _On peut être jaloux, mais à ce point, c'est du dernier ridicule!_"

Levin turned sharply, walked away from him into the depths of the avenue, and went on pacing up and down alone. Soon he heard the rumble of the trap, and through the trees he saw Vassenka, sitting in the hay (unluckily there had been no seat in the trap), in his Scotch cap, being driven down the avenue, jolting over the ruts.

"What's this?" Levin thought, when a footman ran out of the house and stopped the trap. It was the mechanic — Levin had completely forgotten him. The mechanic, bowing low, said something to Veslovsky, then climbed into the trap, and they drove off together.

Stepan Arkadyevitch and the princess were thoroughly upset by what Levin had done. And Levin himself felt not only thoroughly _ridicule_ but utterly in the wrong and disgraced. But when he remembered what he and his wife had been through, and asked himself how he would behave another time, he answered that he would do exactly the same thing again.

Despite all of this, by the end of that day everyone except the princess — who couldn't forgive Levin's behavior — became extraordinarily lively and good-humored, like children after a scolding or grown-ups after a long, formal reception, so that by evening Vassenka's dismissal was talked about, out of the princess's hearing, as if it had been some remote event. And Dolly, who had inherited her father's gift for telling a funny story, made Varenka helpless with laughter as she told for the third and fourth time, always with fresh comic touches, how she had only just put on her new shoes for the visitor's benefit, and on going into the drawing room had suddenly heard the rumble of the trap. And who should be in it but Vassenka himself, with his Scotch cap, his songs and his gaiters, sitting in the hay.

"If only you'd had the carriage brought out! But no — and then I heard: 'Stop!' Oh, I thought, they've relented. I look out, and behold — a fat German being seated beside him, and off they go.... And my new shoes wasted!..."

title: Chapter 16
paragraphs: Darya Alexandrovna stuck to her plan and went to see Anna. She hated to upset her sister and to do anything Levin disapproved of. She fully understood that the Levins were right not to want anything to do with Vronsky. But she felt she had to go and see Anna, and to show her that her feelings could not change just because Anna's situation had. To keep the trip independent of the Levins, Darya Alexandrovna sent into the village to hire horses for the drive; but Levin, hearing of it, went to her to object.

"What makes you think I dislike your going? Even if I did dislike it, I would dislike your refusing to take my horses even more," he said. "You never told me you'd definitely settled on going. Hiring in the village makes me uncomfortable, and what's more important, they'll take the job on and never actually get you there. I have horses. And if you don't want to hurt my feelings, you'll take mine."

Darya Alexandrovna had to give in, and on the appointed day Levin had a team of four horses, with relays, ready for his sister-in-law — pulled together from the farm and the saddle horses, not at all a smart-looking set, but enough to get her the whole way in a day. At a moment when horses were needed for the princess, who was leaving, and for the midwife, putting the team together was no small task for Levin, but the duty of a host would not let him allow Darya Alexandrovna to hire horses while she was a guest in his house. He also knew perfectly well that the twenty roubles such a trip would cost was a serious matter for her; Darya Alexandrovna's financial situation, which was a mess, was a concern the Levins took as if it were their own.

On Levin's advice, Darya Alexandrovna set out before daybreak. The road was good, the carriage comfortable, the horses trotted along cheerfully, and on the box, beside the coachman, sat the counting-house clerk whom Levin was sending along instead of a groom, for safety. Darya Alexandrovna dozed and didn't wake up until they reached the inn where the horses were to be changed.

After drinking tea at the same prosperous peasant's where Levin had stayed on the way to Sviazhsky's, and chatting with the women about their children and with the old man about Count Vronsky, whom he praised very highly, Darya Alexandrovna at ten o'clock went on again. At home, with the children to look after, she had no time to think. So now, four hours into this journey, all the thoughts she had been pushing down before came swarming into her head, and she went over her whole life as she never had before, and from every possible angle. Her own thoughts struck her as strange. At first she thought about the children, who worried her, though the princess and Kitty (she was counting more on Kitty) had promised to look after them. "If only Masha doesn't start her naughty tricks, if only Grisha doesn't get kicked by a horse, if only Lily's stomach doesn't go wrong again!" she thought. But these immediate concerns gave way to questions about the near future. She started thinking about how she had to find a new flat in Moscow for the coming winter, replace the drawing-room furniture, and have a cloak made for her oldest girl. Then questions about the more distant future came up: how she was to place her children in the world. "The girls are all right," she thought; "but the boys?"

"It's all very well that I'm teaching Grisha, but only because I'm free right now — I'm not carrying a child. Stiva, of course, you can't count on. With the help of kind friends I can bring them up; but what if there's another baby on the way?..." And it struck her how untruly it had been said that the curse on woman was that in sorrow she should bring forth children.

"The birth itself is nothing — it's the months of carrying the child that are unbearable," she thought, picturing her last pregnancy and the death of the last baby. And she remembered the conversation she had just had with the young woman at the inn. Asked whether she had any children, the handsome young woman had answered cheerfully:
"I had a little girl, but God set me free; I buried her last Lent."
"And did you grieve very much for her?" Darya Alexandrovna asked.
"Why grieve? The old man has grandchildren enough as it is. It was just a trouble. No working, no nothing. Only a tie."

The answer had struck Darya Alexandrovna as revolting, despite the kind, pleasing face of the young woman; but now she could not help recalling the words. In that cynical phrase there really was a grain of truth.

"Yes, taken altogether," thought Darya Alexandrovna, looking back over her whole existence during those fifteen years of married life, "pregnancy, sickness, mental dullness, indifference to everything, and most of all — ugliness. Kitty, young and pretty as she is, even Kitty has lost her looks; and when I'm carrying a child I become hideous, I know it. The birth, the agony, those hideous agonies, that last moment ... then the nursing, the sleepless nights, the awful pains...."

Darya Alexandrovna shuddered at the mere memory of the pain from cracked breasts she had had with almost every child. "Then the children's illnesses, that constant fear; then bringing them up; bad tendencies" (she thought of little Masha's offense among the raspberries), "education, Latin — it's all so incomprehensible and so hard. And on top of all that, the death of these children." And once again the cruel memory rose in her imagination, the memory that always tore at her mother's heart — the death of her last little baby, who had died of croup; his funeral, the cold indifference of everyone around the little pink coffin, and her own broken heart and lonely anguish at the sight of the pale little brow with its prominent temples, and the open, wondering little mouth, as she had seen it in the coffin the moment before it was covered with the little pink lid with its braided cross.

"And all of this — what's it for? What comes out of it all? That I'm throwing my life away, never a moment's peace, either pregnant or nursing a child, forever irritable, peevish, miserable myself and tormenting others, repulsive to my husband, while the children grow up unhappy, badly educated, and without a penny. Even right now, if it weren't for spending the summer with the Levins, I can't think how we'd be managing to live. Of course Kostya and Kitty are tactful enough that we don't feel it; but it can't go on. They'll have children of their own, they won't be able to keep us; it's a drag on them as it is. How is papa, who has almost nothing left for himself, supposed to help us? So I can't even bring the children up on my own, and may find it hard even with other people's help, at the cost of humiliation. Even granting the best luck — that the children don't die, and that I bring them up somehow. At best they'll just be decent people. That's all I can hope for. And to get even that — what suffering, what slogging!... A whole life ruined!" Again she remembered what the young peasant woman had said, and again the thought disgusted her; but she could not help admitting that in that brutal phrase there was a grain of truth.
"Is it far now, Mihail?" Darya Alexandrovna asked the counting-house clerk, to push her mind off thoughts that were beginning to frighten her.

"From this village, they say, it's five miles." The carriage drove down the village street and onto a bridge. On the bridge stood a crowd of peasant women with coils of binding for the sheaves on their shoulders, chattering loudly and cheerfully. They stood still on the bridge and stared curiously at the carriage. Every face turned toward Darya Alexandrovna looked healthy and happy, and she envied them their enjoyment of life. "They're all living, all enjoying life," Darya Alexandrovna kept thinking, after they had passed the peasant women and were trotting uphill again, comfortably seated on the soft springs of the old carriage. "While I — let out, as it were, from prison, from a world of worries that grinds me to death — am only able to look around for a moment. They are all living: those peasant women, my sister Natalia, and Varenka, and Anna, whom I'm on my way to see — all of them, but not me.

"And they go after Anna. What for? Am I any better? I, at any rate, have a husband I love — not the way I'd like to love him, but I do love him, while Anna never loved hers. How is she to blame? She wants to live. God put that in our hearts. It's very likely I would have done the same. Even now I don't feel sure I did the right thing in listening to her at that terrible time when she came to me in Moscow. I should have left my husband then and started my life over. I might have loved, and been loved, for real. And is what I have now any better? I don't respect him. He's necessary to me," she thought about her husband, "and I put up with him. Is that any better? At that time I could still have been admired, I still had my looks," Darya Alexandrovna pursued her thoughts, and she would have liked to see herself in a mirror. She had a traveling mirror in her bag and she wanted to take it out; but, looking at the backs of the coachman and the swaying counting-house clerk, she felt she would be embarrassed if either of them happened to look around, and she did not take it out.

But without looking in the glass, she thought that even now it was not too late; and she thought of Sergey Ivanovitch, who had always been particularly attentive to her, of Stiva's good-hearted friend Turovtsin, who had helped her nurse her children through scarlatina and was in love with her. And there was someone else, a quite young man, who — her husband had told her, as a joke — thought her more beautiful than either of her sisters. And the most passionate and impossible romances rose up before Darya Alexandrovna's imagination. "Anna did exactly right, and I'll certainly never reproach her for it. She's happy, she's making another person happy, and she's not broken down the way I am — she's most likely just the way she always was: bright, clever, open to every impression," thought Darya Alexandrovna — and a sly smile curved her lips, because as she thought over Anna's love affair, Darya Alexandrovna was constructing on parallel lines an almost identical love affair for herself, with an imaginary composite figure, the ideal man who was in love with her. She, like Anna, confessed the whole thing to her husband. And the astonishment and bewilderment of Stepan Arkadyevitch at this confession made her smile.
In these daydreams she reached the turning of the high road that led to Vozdvizhenskoe.

title: Chapter 17
paragraphs: The coachman pulled up his four horses and looked off to the right, toward a field of rye where some peasants were sitting on a cart. The counting-house clerk was about to jump down, but on second thought he shouted sharply to the peasants instead and waved them over. The wind that had seemed to blow as they drove dropped the moment the carriage stopped; gadflies settled on the steaming horses, which shook them off angrily. The metallic clink of a whetstone against a scythe, drifting over from the cart, stopped. One of the peasants got up and came toward the carriage.
"Well, you are slow!" the counting-house clerk shouted impatiently at the peasant, who was stepping carefully on his bare feet over the ruts of the rough, dry road. "Come on, hurry up!"
A curly-haired old man with a strip of bast tied around his hair, his bent back dark with sweat, came toward the carriage at a quicker pace and laid his sunburnt hand on the mud-guard.

"Vozdvizhenskoe — the manor house? The count's place?" he repeated. "Go on to the end of this track, then turn left. Straight along the avenue and you'll come right on it. But who is it you want? The count himself?"
"Well, are they at home, my good man?" Darya Alexandrovna asked vaguely, not knowing how to ask about Anna even of this peasant.

"At home, for sure," the peasant said, shifting from one bare foot to the other and leaving a clear print of five toes and a heel in the dust. "Sure to be at home," he repeated, clearly eager to talk. "Visitors arrived only yesterday. There's quite a crowd of visitors. What do you want?" He turned around and called to a lad, who was shouting something to him from the cart. "Oh! They all rode by here not long ago, to look at a reaping machine. They'll be home by now. And who would you belong to?..."
"We've come a long way," said the coachman, climbing back up onto the box. "So it's not far?"
"I tell you, it's right here. As soon as you get past...." he said, still holding on to the carriage.
A healthy-looking, broad-shouldered young fellow came up too.
"What — is it laborers they want for the harvest?" he asked.
"I don't know, my boy."
"So you keep to the left, and you'll come straight on it," said the peasant, clearly reluctant to let the travelers go, eager to keep talking.
The coachman started the horses, but they had only just begun to turn off when the peasant shouted: "Stop! Hi, friend! Stop!" the two voices called. The coachman stopped.
"They're coming! There they are!" the peasant shouted. "See what a turn-out!" he said, pointing to four people on horseback and two in a _char-à-banc_ coming along the road.
It was Vronsky with a jockey, Veslovsky and Anna on horseback, and Princess Varvara and Sviazhsky in the _char-à-banc_. They had gone out to look at a new reaping machine in action.

When the carriage stopped, the riders were coming up at a walk. Anna was in front, beside Veslovsky. Anna, walking her horse — a sturdy English cob with a cropped mane and short tail — quietly, her beautiful head and black hair straying loose under her high hat, her full shoulders, her slim waist in the black riding habit, all the ease and grace of her bearing — made an impression on Dolly.

For the first moment it seemed to her improper that Anna should be on horseback. In Darya Alexandrovna's mind, riding for a lady was tied to ideas of girlish flirtation and frivolity, which, in her view, didn't suit Anna's situation. But when she had taken a closer look at her, she was reconciled at once to her riding. For all the elegance, everything about Anna's posture, dress, and movement was so simple, quiet, and dignified that nothing could have been more natural.
