Beside Anna, on a hot-looking gray cavalry horse, sat Vassenka Veslovsky in his Scotch cap with floating ribbons, his stout legs stuck out in front of him, plainly delighted with himself. Darya Alexandrovna couldn't help smiling good-naturedly as she recognized him. Behind them rode Vronsky on a dark bay mare that was obviously hot from galloping. He was holding her in, pulling on the reins.
Behind him came a small man in a jockey's outfit. Sviazhsky and Princess Varvara, in a new _char-à-banc_ with a big, raven-black trotter, overtook the riders.

Anna's face suddenly lit up with a delighted smile the moment she recognized, in the small figure huddled in the corner of the old carriage, Dolly. She cried out, started in the saddle, and put her horse into a gallop. When she reached the carriage she jumped down without help, and holding up her riding habit she ran over to greet Dolly.

"I thought it was you and didn't dare let myself think so. How lovely! You can't imagine how glad I am!" she said, one moment pressing her face against Dolly's and kissing her, the next holding her at arm's length and looking her over with a smile.
"Here's a wonderful surprise, Alexey!" she said, glancing back at Vronsky, who had dismounted and was walking up to them.
Vronsky, taking off his tall gray hat, came up to Dolly.
"You can't imagine how glad we are to see you," he said, giving the words a particular weight, and showing his strong white teeth in a smile.
Vassenka Veslovsky, without getting off his horse, lifted his cap and saluted the visitor by cheerfully waving the ribbons over his head.
"That is Princess Varvara," Anna said, answering a questioning glance from Dolly as the _char-à-banc_ pulled up.
"Ah!" said Darya Alexandrovna, and her face involuntarily showed her displeasure.

Princess Varvara was her husband's aunt; Dolly had known her a long time, and did not respect her. She knew Princess Varvara had spent her whole life sponging on her wealthy relatives, but the fact that she was now sponging on Vronsky — a man who was nothing to her — mortified Dolly on her husband's account, given the family connection. Anna noticed Dolly's expression and was thrown by it. She blushed, let go of her riding habit, and stumbled over it.

Darya Alexandrovna went up to the _char-à-banc_ and greeted Princess Varvara coolly. Sviazhsky she also knew. He asked after his odd friend with the young wife, and, running his eye over the mismatched horses and the carriage with its patched mud-guards, proposed that the ladies get into the _char-à-banc_.
"And I'll get into this vehicle," he said. "The horse is quiet, and the princess drives capitally."
"No, stay where you are," Anna said, coming up, "and we'll go in the carriage," and, taking Dolly's arm, she led her off.

Darya Alexandrovna's eyes were dazzled by the elegant carriage of a kind she had never seen before, the splendid horses, the elegant and glamorous people around her. But what struck her most was the change in Anna, whom she knew so well and loved. Another woman, less observant, who hadn't known Anna before, or who hadn't been thinking the kinds of thoughts Darya Alexandrovna had been thinking on the road, would not have noticed anything special. But now Dolly was struck by that temporary beauty that only shows itself in women in the moments of love, and that she now saw in Anna's face. Everything about her face — the clearly marked dimples in her cheeks and chin, the line of her lips, the smile that seemed to flicker across her face, the brightness of her eyes, the grace and quickness of her movements, the fullness of her voice, even the way she answered Veslovsky, with a sort of angry friendliness, when he asked permission to get on her cob to teach it to gallop with the right leg first — all of it was peculiarly captivating, and it seemed she was aware of it herself and taking pleasure in it.

When the two women were seated in the carriage, a sudden awkwardness came over both of them. Anna was thrown by the searching, inquiring look Dolly fixed on her. Dolly was embarrassed because after Sviazhsky's remark about "this vehicle," she couldn't help feeling ashamed of the dirty old carriage Anna was sitting in with her. Philip the coachman and the counting-house clerk felt the same way. The counting-house clerk, to cover his embarrassment, busied himself settling the ladies, but Philip the coachman turned sullen and was bracing himself not to be cowed in future by this outward superiority. He smiled ironically at the raven horse and was already deciding, privately, that this smart trotter in the _char-à-banc_ was only any good for _promenage_ and couldn't possibly do thirty miles straight off in the heat.
The peasants had all gotten up from the cart and were watching the meeting of the friends with curiosity and amusement, passing comments on it.
"They look pleased — haven't seen each other for a long while," said the curly-haired old man with the bast around his hair.
"I say, Uncle Gerasim, if we could borrow that raven horse to cart the corn — that would be quick work!"
"Look there! Is that a woman in breeches?" said one of them, pointing to Vassenka Veslovsky sitting in a side saddle.
"No — a man! See how smartly he's at it!"
"Eh, lads — looks like we won't be sleeping today after all?"
"No chance of any sleep today!" said the old man, with a sidelong look at the sun. "Midday's gone by, look there! Pick up your hooks and come on!"

title: Chapter 18
paragraphs: Anna looked at Dolly's thin, careworn face, its wrinkles filled with road dust, and was about to say what she was thinking — that Dolly had grown thinner. But, aware that she herself had grown handsomer, and that Dolly's eyes were telling her so, she sighed and began to talk about herself instead.

"You are looking at me," she said, "and wondering how I can be happy in my position. Well — it's shameful to admit, but I — I am inexcusably happy. Something magical has happened to me, like a dream where you are terrified, panic-stricken, and then suddenly you wake and all the horrors are gone. I have waked. I have lived through the misery, the dread, and now for a long time, especially since we have been here, I have been so happy!..." she said, looking at Dolly with a timid, questioning smile.
"How glad I am!" said Dolly, smiling, speaking more coolly than she meant to. "I am very glad for you. Why haven't you written to me?"
"Why?... Because I hadn't the courage.... You forget my position...."
"To me? Hadn't the courage? If you knew how I — how I look at...."
Darya Alexandrovna wanted to put into words what she had been thinking that morning, but somehow, just now, it felt out of place.

"But we'll talk about that later. What is this — what are all these buildings?" she asked, wanting to change the subject and pointing at the red and green roofs that had appeared behind the green hedges of acacia and lilac. "It's almost a little town."
But Anna did not answer.
"No, no! How do you look at my position — what do you think of it?" she asked.

"I think...." Darya Alexandrovna began, but at that instant Vassenka Veslovsky, having gotten the cob to canter with the right leg leading, galloped past them, bumping heavily up and down in his short jacket on the chamois leather of the side saddle. "He's doing it, Anna Arkadyevna!" he shouted.
Anna did not so much as glance at him; but it once again seemed inappropriate to Darya Alexandrovna to begin so long a conversation in the carriage, and so she cut her thought short.
"I don't think anything," she said, "but I have always loved you, and if you love someone, you love the whole person, just as they are and not as you might wish them to be...."

Anna took her eyes off her friend's face and dropped her eyelids (a new habit Dolly had not seen in her before), and considered, trying to take in the full meaning of the words. Then, obviously interpreting them as she wished, she looked back at Dolly.
"If you had any sins," she said, "they would all be forgiven you for coming to see me and for saying that."
And Dolly saw that tears stood in her eyes. She pressed Anna's hand in silence.
"Well — and what are these buildings? There are so many of them!" After a moment's silence she repeated her question.

"These are the servants' houses, the barns, the stables," Anna answered. "And there the park begins. It had all gone to ruin, but Alexey has had everything renewed. He loves this place, and — what I never expected — he has become deeply interested in managing it. But his is such a rich nature! Whatever he takes up, he does splendidly. Far from being bored by it, he works at it with passion. He — with the temperament I know in him — has become careful and businesslike, a first-rate manager. He counts every kopeck in running the estate. But only there. When it comes to tens of thousands, he gives money no thought at all." She spoke with that gleefully sly smile women so often have when they speak of the secret traits that only they know in the men they love. "Do you see that big building? That is the new hospital. I think it will cost more than a hundred thousand; it is his current passion. And do you know how it all came about? The peasants asked him for some meadowland at a cheaper rate, I think it was, and he refused, and I accused him of being stingy. Of course it wasn't really because of that — it was all of a piece — but he began this hospital to prove, you see, that he was not miserly about money. _C'est une petitesse_, if you like, but I love him all the more for it. And now you'll see the house in a moment. It was his grandfather's house, and he has had nothing changed outside."
"How beautiful!" said Dolly, looking with involuntary admiration at the handsome columned house, which stood out against the different shades of green of the old trees in the garden.
"Isn't it fine? And from the top of the house, the view is magnificent."
They drove into a gravel courtyard bright with flowers, where two laborers were laying a stone edging around the light loam of a flowerbed, and pulled up under a covered porch.

"Ah, they're back already!" said Anna, looking at the saddle horses, which were just being led away from the steps. "He's a nice horse, isn't he? That's my cob — my favorite. Bring him over and bring me some sugar. Where is the count?" she asked of two smart footmen who darted out. "Ah, there he is!" she said, seeing Vronsky coming to meet her with Veslovsky.

"Where are you going to put the princess?" Vronsky said to Anna in French, and without waiting for a reply he greeted Darya Alexandrovna again, and this time kissed her hand. "The big balcony room, I think."
"Oh, no — that's too far off. Better the corner room; we shall see more of each other. Come, let's go up," Anna said, as she gave her favorite horse the sugar the footman had brought.
"_Et vous oubliez votre devoir_," she said to Veslovsky, who had come out onto the steps as well.
"_Pardon, j'en ai tout plein les poches_," he answered, smiling, putting his fingers into his waistcoat pocket.
"_Mais vous venez trop tard_," she said, wiping her hand with her handkerchief — the horse had wet it taking the sugar.
Anna turned to Dolly. "You can stay a while? Only one day? That's impossible!"
"I promised to be back, and the children...." Dolly said, embarrassed both because she had to get her bag out of the carriage and because she knew her face was covered in dust.
"No, Dolly, darling!... Well, we'll see. Come along, come along!" and Anna led Dolly to her room.

It was not the smart guest chamber Vronsky had suggested, but the one Anna had said Dolly would have to excuse. And this room, which apparently needed excusing, was more lavish than any Dolly had ever stayed in — a luxury that reminded her of the best hotels abroad.

"Well, darling, how happy I am!" Anna said, still in her riding habit, sitting down for a moment beside Dolly. "Tell me about all of you. I only caught a glimpse of Stiva, and he can't tell anyone about the children. How is my favorite, Tanya? Quite a big girl by now, I expect?"
"Yes, she's very tall," Darya Alexandrovna answered shortly, surprised at how coolly she was responding about her children. "We are having a lovely stay at the Levins'."

"Oh, if I'd only known," Anna said, "that you don't despise me!... You could all have come here together. Stiva's an old friend of ours, and a close one of Alexey's, you know," she added, and abruptly blushed.
"Yes, but we are all...." Dolly answered, flustered.

"But in my joy I'm talking nonsense. The main thing, darling, is that I am so glad you're here!" said Anna, kissing her again. "You still haven't told me what you think of me, and I keep wanting to know. But I'm glad you'll see me as I am. The one thing I shouldn't want is for people to imagine I am trying to prove anything. I don't want to prove anything; I only want to live — to do no one any harm but myself. I have the right to do that, haven't I? But it is a big subject, and we'll talk it all through properly later. Now I'll go and dress, and send a maid to you."

title: Chapter 19
paragraphs: Left alone, Darya Alexandrovna scanned the room with a good housewife's eye. Everything she had seen on her way through the house, and everything she saw now in her room, gave her an impression of wealth and sumptuousness, of that modern European luxury she had only read about in English novels and never seen in Russia, certainly not in the country. Everything was new — from the new French hangings on the walls to the carpet that covered the whole floor. The bed had a spring mattress, and a special kind of bolster, and silk pillowcases on the little pillows. The marble washstand, the dressing table, the small sofa, the side tables, the bronze clock on the chimney piece, the window curtains, and the _portières_ were all new and expensive.

The smart maid who came in to offer her services — hair piled high, a gown smarter than Dolly's — was as new and expensive as the room itself. Darya Alexandrovna liked her neatness, her deferential and helpful manner, but she felt uneasy in her presence. She was ashamed to have her see the patched dressing jacket that had been packed for her by mistake. She was ashamed of the very patches and darns she had been so proud of at home. At home it had been perfectly clear that for six dressing jackets one needed twenty-four yards of nainsook at sixteen pence the yard, which came to thirty shillings, plus the cutting and the sewing — and that thirty shillings had been saved. But in front of the maid she felt, if not exactly ashamed, then certainly uncomfortable.
Darya Alexandrovna was hugely relieved when Annushka, whom she had known for years, walked in. The smart maid was summoned to her mistress, and Annushka stayed with Darya Alexandrovna.

Annushka was obviously delighted at Dolly's arrival and started chattering away without a pause. Dolly noticed that she was longing to share her opinion of her mistress's situation, especially the count's love and devotion to Anna Arkadyevna, but Dolly carefully cut her off whenever she began on that.
"I grew up with Anna Arkadyevna; my lady is dearer to me than anything. Well, it's not for us to judge. And there does seem to be so much love...."
"Be so good as to pour out the water now, please, so I can wash," Darya Alexandrovna cut her short.
"Of course. We keep two women just for washing the small things, but most of the linen is done by machine. The count looks into everything himself. Ah, what a husband!..."
Dolly was glad when Anna came in and put a stop to Annushka's gossip.
Anna had put on a very simple batiste gown. Dolly studied that simple gown closely. She knew what it meant — and what such simplicity cost.
"An old friend," Anna said of Annushka.

Anna was no longer flustered. She was perfectly composed, perfectly at ease. Dolly saw that she had now fully recovered from the impression of her arrival, and had taken on that surface, careless tone which, as it were, closed the door on the compartment that held her deeper feelings and thoughts.
"Well, Anna, and how is your little girl?" Dolly asked.

"Annie?" (That was what she called her little daughter, Anna.) "Very well. She has come along wonderfully. Would you like to see her? Come, I'll show her to you. We had a dreadful time of it," she went on, "over nurses. We had an Italian wet-nurse. A good creature, but so stupid! We wanted to be rid of her, but the baby is so used to her that we've gone on keeping her."
"But how have you managed?..." Dolly was about to ask what surname the little girl would carry; but, noticing a sudden frown on Anna's face, she shifted course.
"How did you manage? Have you weaned her yet?"
But Anna had understood.

"That isn't what you meant to ask, is it? You meant to ask about her surname. Yes? It worries Alexey. She has no name — that is, she is a Karenina," said Anna, dropping her eyelids until nothing showed but the lashes meeting. "But we'll talk about all that later," she said, her face suddenly brightening. "Come, I'll show you. _Elle est très gentille_. She crawls now."

In the nursery, the luxury that had struck Dolly throughout the house struck her even more. There were little go-carts ordered from England, and contraptions for learning to walk, and a sofa shaped like a billiard table, made specifically for crawling, and swings and baths, all of special design and all up to date. They were all English, sturdy, and well made, and obviously very expensive. The room was large, very bright, and very high-ceilinged.

When they walked in, the baby — wearing nothing but her little smock — was sitting in a small armchair at the table, having her dinner of broth, which she was spilling all over her chest. The baby was being fed, and the Russian nursemaid was clearly sharing the meal. Neither the wet-nurse nor the head nurse was there; they were in the next room, from which came the sound of their conversation in the strange French that was their only common language.

Hearing Anna's voice, a smart, tall English nurse with a disagreeable face and a dissolute look came through the door, hurriedly shaking her fair curls, and at once began defending herself, though Anna had said nothing critical. At every word Anna said, the English nurse said hurriedly, several times over, "Yes, my lady."

The rosy baby, with her black eyebrows and dark hair, her sturdy red little body and its tight goose-flesh skin, delighted Darya Alexandrovna in spite of the cross look the child fixed on the stranger. She positively envied the baby's robust health. She was delighted, too, with how the baby crawled. None of her own children had crawled like that. When the baby was set down on the carpet and her little dress was tucked up behind, she was wonderfully charming. She looked around like some small wild animal at the grown-ups with her bright black eyes, smiled — clearly pleased that they were admiring her — and, with her legs splayed sideways, pushed strongly on her arms, then quickly drew her whole back up after them, and made another little advance forward on her arms.

But the whole atmosphere of the nursery, and especially the English nurse, Darya Alexandrovna did not like at all. The only way she could explain to herself how Anna, with her insight into people, could have taken on so unprepossessing, so disreputable-looking a woman as nurse to her child was to assume that no good nurse would have agreed to enter a household as irregular as Anna's.

Besides, from a few stray remarks, Darya Alexandrovna saw at once that Anna, the two nurses, and the child shared no common life, and that the mother's visit was something out of the ordinary. Anna wanted to fetch a plaything for the baby and couldn't find it.
Most astonishing of all was that when Anna was asked how many teeth the baby had, she answered wrong and knew nothing about the two newest ones.

"Sometimes I feel sorry I am so superfluous here," Anna said, leaving the nursery and lifting her skirt to step around the plaything that stood in the doorway. "It was very different with my first child."
"I would have expected the opposite," said Darya Alexandrovna shyly.

"Oh, no! By the way, do you know I saw Seryozha?" Anna said, narrowing her eyes as though looking at something far off. "But we'll talk about that later. You wouldn't believe it — I'm like a hungry beggar woman in front of a full dinner. I don't know what to start on first. The dinner is you, and the conversations I have ahead of me with you, which I could never have with anyone else; and I can't decide which subject to begin on. _Mais je ne vous ferai grâce de rien_. I must have everything out with you."

"Oh, I really ought to give you a sketch of the company you'll meet here," she went on. "I'll start with the ladies. Princess Varvara — you know her, and I know what you and Stiva think of her. Stiva says the entire purpose of her life is to prove her superiority over Auntie Katerina Pavlovna: all true; but she's a good-hearted woman, and I am so grateful to her. In Petersburg there was a moment when I absolutely had to have a chaperone. And then she turned up. But really, she is good-hearted. She did a great deal to ease my position. I see you don't grasp the whole difficulty of my position — there, in Petersburg," she added. "Here I am perfectly at ease and happy. Well, more on that later. Then Sviazhsky — he is the marshal of the district, a very decent sort of man, but he wants something out of Alexey. You understand: with his land, now that we are settled in the country, Alexey can wield great influence. Then there's Tushkevitch — you've met him, you know him — Betsy's admirer. Now he has been dropped and he has come to see us. As Alexey says, he is one of those people who are very pleasant so long as you accept them as what they try to appear to be, _et puis il est comme il faut_, as Princess Varvara says. Then Veslovsky... you know him. A nice boy," she said, and a sly smile curved her lips. "What's this wild story about him and the Levins? Veslovsky told Alexey, and we don't believe a word of it. _Il est très gentil et naïf_," she said, smiling again. "Men need something to do, and Alexey needs a circle, so I value all these people. We have to keep the house lively and amusing, so that Alexey will not long for something new. Then you'll meet the steward — a German, a very good man, and he understands his work. Alexey thinks very highly of him. Then the doctor, a young man — not quite a Nihilist, perhaps, but, you know, eats with his knife... still, a very good doctor. Then the architect.... _Une petite cour!_"
